theory.headline_finding: Eisfeldt–Rampini does not falsify the operator's mechanism, but a different result in the same literature comes much closer, and it has been missed. Kermani & Ma (2020) show that cyclical conditions move liquidation recovery rates by only about five to ten percentage points, whereas fixed physical attributes of an asset (mobility, durability, customisation) explain roughly 40% of cross-industry variation and generate recovery rates ranging from near 70% (transportation) to under 10% (some services). The bust is therefore a second-order determinant of the price at which capacity changes hands; specificity is first-order. The claim "the bubble made the capacity cheap" is largely wrong — the capacity was always going to be cheap in any alternative use. Worse for the framework: Ramey & Shapiro (2001) find that displaced aerospace capital sold to *industry insiders* at a 29–40% premium over outsiders (up to roughly 100% for newer machine tools), and Shleifer & Vishny (1992) explain why. If insiders are always the high-value users, then "L3 is different people" is not a signature of the mechanism working — it is the standard finance signature of an allocative *loss*. The operator's framework and the fire-sale literature predict the same observable (assets exiting the incumbent class in a bust) with opposite welfare signs, and the framework currently has no way to tell them apart. That is a second indexing problem sitting alongside the layer-assignment problem round 1 identified.
theory.analysis:
## 1. What Eisfeldt–Rampini actually establishes, at full strength

The result is robust and has survived sixteen extra years of data. Eisfeldt & Shi (NBER w25085, 2018), updating Eisfeldt & Rampini (2006), report a correlation of 0.58 between the cyclical components of capital reallocation and GDP, significant at 1%. Boom years (GDP above HP trend) show roughly a 50% higher reallocation rate. Mean turnover is 1.96% of the capital stock annually; reallocation is about 28% of total investment for US public firms. Measured *benefits* to reallocation move the other way or not at all: firm-level Tobin's q dispersion has no significant cyclical correlation, TFP-growth dispersion across industries is acyclical, capacity-utilisation dispersion is significantly countercyclical. Their inference: the frictions blocking reallocation must be countercyclical.

Three satellite results make it worse for the operator. Lanteri (AER 2018) shows used-capital *prices* are procyclical and more volatile than new-capital prices, and that high-productivity firms after a negative shock prefer *new* capital because used capital is an imperfect substitute under firm-level specificity — the exact opposite of the L3-buys-distressed-L2-assets story. Ottonello (2017) documents "capital unemployment": more structures sit *vacant* after negative financial shocks. Cui (2017) shows tightened borrowing constraints can *prevent* low-productivity firms from exiting, because falling leverage reduces debt overhang and raises the option value of staying alive. Kehrig (2015) is the sharpest cut: establishment-level productivity dispersion is countercyclical, but the increase is driven by a *higher share of low-productivity establishments*. The recession is populating the left tail. It is not generating a queue of frustrated high-productivity buyers.

Taken together: in a bust, less capital moves, at lower prices, to fewer buyers, while the assets that should move sit idle and the incumbents that should die survive. Any framework asserting that busts are the moment capacity productively changes hands has to answer this.

## 2. Reconciliations that do not work

**"They measured the wrong frequency."** True but thin. HP-filtering removes the low-frequency component where the operator's mechanism lives, and E–R aggregate over all public firms while the operator cares about one collapsing sector. This is a "you measured a different thing" defence; it creates room for the mechanism without providing any evidence for it.

**"Network infrastructure has no alternative use, so it behaves differently."** As usually stated this is backwards and makes the framework *worse*. Kermani & Ma find explicitly that in industries with lower PPE recovery rates, firms make *fewer* PPE sales, in both frequency and dollar amount. Ramey & Shapiro's largest estimated discount of anything they measured was on structures — α = 0.96, standard error 0.019 — and the three plants did not sell their buildings at all, because bringing them to environmental standards cost more than the sale price, so they were razed. Bernstein, Colonnelli & Iverson (JF 2019) find that liquidated firms' assets show *lower* long-run utilisation than reorganised firms', concentrated in thin markets and areas with poor finance access. Benmelech (RFS 2009) finds non-standard track gauge reduced railroads' debt capacity and maturity precisely because rolling stock and track were unsalable to anyone with a different gauge — and that potential demand collapsed further when many railroads entered receivership simultaneously. Gavazza (JPE 2011) finds thin-market assets are held longer, at lower utilisation and lower average productivity. Every one of these says: the more network-like and specific the asset, the *worse* the reallocation outcome. Low alternative use predicts idling, not handover.

## 3. The reconciliation that does work, stated precisely

The entire empirical literature measures one construct: **physical redeployability — can the asset perform a *different job*?** Kim & Kung (RFS 2017) operationalise it as the count of industries using an asset class, from the BEA 1997 capital flow table (180 asset classes, 123 industries), aggregated to industry and then to firm via segments. Kermani & Ma decompose it into mobility (transport cost), durability (depreciation rate), and standardisation (design-cost share), which jointly explain ~40% of recovery-rate variation; they note that with zero transport cost, zero depreciation and zero customisation the implied recovery rate is 100%. Ramey & Shapiro measure it directly as α, and their canonical illustration is a wind tunnel capable of 270 mph sold to a firm renting it out at low speeds to bicycle-helmet designers — the characteristic that made the asset expensive is precisely the characteristic the new user does not value.

The operator's cases require nothing of the sort. Dark fibre bought by a content company is carrying photons — exactly what the bankrupt carrier built it to do. There is no redeployment. What changed is the *revenue model wrapped around an unchanged physical function*. Call this **commercial redeployability**, and note it is near-orthogonal to the measured construct. No paper in this literature measures it, because the natural experiments they use (aerospace downsizing, railroad receivership, airline distress) are all cases where physical output demand *fell*.

This yields the discriminator the framework has been missing:

> **The mechanism applies if and only if the shock kills the revenue model while physical demand for the asset's output survives or grows. It fails whenever the shock kills demand for the output itself.**

Ramey & Shapiro's setting fails this test by construction: real defence purchases of aerospace equipment rose 225% from 1977 to 1988 and then fell back to 1977 levels by 1995 (their Figure 1). Demand for the *output* died. Machine tools went to lower-value uses, insiders paid a premium because they were still the highest-value users, and the measured 28-cents-on-the-dollar average q reflects a genuine real loss. The framework should correctly predict no third generation there, and there was none. Telecom post-2001 passes: traffic kept compounding while the belief that you could charge 1999 prices for it died. Single-mode glass installed in the 1990s still carries traffic today, and capacity has been multiplied by replacing only the short-lived DWDM terminal electronics — the substrate never needed to change.

This also repairs the Shleifer–Vishny problem rather than dodging it. S–V's engine is v_insider > v_outsider combined with correlated insider distress, which makes bust-time transfer an allocative loss by construction. Model-death *inverts the ordering*: the incumbent class's valuation of the asset collapses toward zero while an outsider class with a different cost structure values it highly. Outsiders become the high-value buyers. That is a rare configuration, which is exactly why the framework has so few clean cases.

## 4. The correct restatement of L2's role

Ramey & Shapiro supply the missing microfoundation, and it is not the one the operator assumes. Because resale discounts are enormous, the option value of installed capital is very high, so firms rationally hold: one of their plants ran at very low output for nearly a decade rather than sell. Their conclusion is that firms sell significant capital only when they decide to cease operations. Cessation is countercyclical. E–R's procyclical aggregate is dominated by going-concern transactions — M&A waves at high valuations, PPE sales by healthy firms — which reshuffle assets *within* the incumbent class and are therefore not the operator's event at all. Procyclical reallocation *volume* is fully consistent with countercyclical *ownership-class turnover*. Nobody has decomposed reallocation this way; the framework is currently unfalsified here rather than confirmed, and this is the single highest-value empirical test available.

So the defensible version of the mechanism is:

> The bubble's contribution is not that it makes capacity cheap — specificity does that, always, and the cycle only moves it 5–10 points. The bubble's contribution is that it makes capacity *exist* in quantities no rational owner would have built, and the bust supplies the only event (cessation of operations) capable of dislodging an asset whose option value would otherwise keep it in incumbent hands indefinitely. The long lag is not gestation; it is search cost, disassembly cost, and the multi-year wind-down Ramey & Shapiro document.

## 5. The redeployability score

Designed to be computable at the frenzy peak. Note it is deliberately **non-monotonic in the finance literature's measure**: high Kim–Kung redeployability predicts the asset is quietly absorbed by adjacent industries with no third generation (Pulvino's aircraft, per Ramey & Shapiro's re-estimation on his data, show α ≈ 0.03, insignificant, implying q ≈ 1 — a perfect asset and a useless L2). The operator wants *low* physical redeployability combined with *high* functional invariance, a narrow corner of the space.

**Hard gate A — Output-demand survival.** Compound growth in physical demand for the asset's *output* from peak to peak+5. Negative ⇒ score 0, framework inapplicable.
**Hard gate B — Reset persistence.** Years to rebuild the capacity at scale, and whether real replacement cost deflates. If an entrant at t+5 rebuilds at equal or lower real cost, the L3 cost-basis advantage is not durable ⇒ 0.

Then seven factors, 0–3 each (max 21):
1. **Functional invariance** — asset performs its original function unchanged, capability upgraded only by swapping cheap short-lived overlay equipment. Proxy: ratio of long-lived immobile substrate cost to programmable overlay cost.
2. **Insider-premium inversion** — signed Ramey–Shapiro λ. Ex-ante proxy: is incumbent unit revenue collapsing faster than the asset's unit output cost?
3. **Buyer-distress decorrelation** (Shleifer–Vishny, Benmelech) — are plausible high-value buyers in a different financing state from sellers? Proxy: correlation of buyer-set and seller-set credit spreads over prior three years.
4. **Market thickness at transaction size** (Gavazza; Bernstein–Colonnelli–Iverson) — count of independent acquirers with balance-sheet capacity ≥ deal size. This deliberately opposes factor 3; thin on both sides yields Ottonello's vacant structures.
5. **Separability from organisational capital** (Kermani–Ma; Kiyotaki–Moore) — does the asset work with a small hireable crew and no tacit process knowledge?
6. **Standards position** (Benmelech's gauge, generalised) — is the substrate standard-agnostic, or stranded on a dying standard?
7. **Encumbrance-free conveyability** — can title pass clean of remediation, decommissioning or service obligations? Ramey & Shapiro's unsold, razed buildings are the zero case.

Threshold: both gates passed and ≥16 = strong; 10–15 = partial; <10 = the overbuild will be scrapped, idled, or absorbed by incumbents.

Calibration: 1990s long-haul fibre ≈ 19, both gates pass. 1990s aerospace plant: gate A fails, 0. Railway Mania track: gates pass but factor 3 = 0 (universal simultaneous receivership) and factor 6 = 1 (gauge), total ≈ 9 — predicting value accrued to consolidating incumbents rather than a distinct third generation, which fits, and fits round 1's finding that the Railway-Time claim was false. 2021 crypto mining rigs: gate B fails, 0. **Sharpest live prediction: applied to the current AI buildout the score splits the asset — GPUs fail gate B outright (≈18-month reproduction, strictly superior successors), while shells, substations, grid interconnects, cooling and powered land pass both gates and score high. The framework's own logic says the third generation inherits the power and the buildings, not the silicon.**
theory.implications_for_framework: QUALIFIES SHARPLY — and forces one substantive retraction plus one addition. The retraction: "the bust makes the capacity cheap" is not supportable. Kermani & Ma show cyclical conditions move recovery rates only 5–10 points while fixed physical attributes explain ~40% of cross-industry variation; specificity, not the cycle, sets the price. L2's causal role must be downgraded from "creates the discount" to "creates the asset in irrational quantity, and supplies the cessation event that dislodges it." The addition: the framework acquires its first genuinely ex-ante falsification criterion, which is a real gain over round 1's unresolved layer-indexing problem. The gate is output-demand survival — the mechanism operates only when the shock kills the revenue model while physical demand for the asset's output survives, and fails whenever the shock kills output demand. This is checkable from one observable series at the time of the bust, is not indexical to where the analyst starts counting, and correctly excludes Ramey & Shapiro's aerospace case (where demand genuinely died and real losses were measured) while admitting fibre. The framework also inherits a new and serious problem it did not know it had: "L3 is different people" is the identical observable that Shleifer–Vishny and Ramey & Shapiro read as evidence of allocative *loss*, since insiders paid a 29–40% premium in the only direct measurement available. The framework cannot keep treating outsider acquisition as self-evidently the mechanism working. It needs the Bernstein–Colonnelli–Iverson test — post-transfer asset utilisation — as its confirmatory step. Finally, Eisfeldt–Rampini itself should be conceded as directionally hostile but not decisive: it measures volume of reallocation, dominated by going-concern transactions within the incumbent class, whereas the framework requires ownership-class turnover, which nobody has measured separately. Claim the reconciliation, but flag it as untested rather than established.

testable_propositions: Ownership-class decomposition: split Eisfeldt–Rampini's reallocation measure into (a) going-concern transactions between solvent firms and (b) transfers arising from cessation, Chapter 7, or s.363 sales. Prediction: (a) carries the entire 0.58 procyclical correlation; (b) is acyclical or countercyclical. If (b) is also procyclical at conventional significance, the reconciliation in section 4 fails and the framework loses its main defence against Eisfeldt–Rampini.

Output-demand gate: across a sample of sectoral capital-stock collapses, code compound growth in physical output demand from peak to peak+5. Prediction: no case with negative output-demand growth produces an identifiable third generation of entrants capturing majority value. Aerospace 1988–95 is the confirming negative; a single counterexample with falling output demand and a genuine third generation falsifies the gate.

Insider-premium sign test: estimate Ramey & Shapiro's λ_insider on asset sales from telecom 2001–04 and from any candidate L2. Prediction: λ_insider is negative (outsiders pay more) in cases the framework claims, and positive in cases it does not. A uniformly positive λ across all cases would mean the framework can never be distinguished from ordinary fire-sale value destruction.

Post-transfer utilisation: apply the Bernstein–Colonnelli–Iverson design (Census establishment data, long-run utilisation) to bust-era infrastructure transfers. Prediction: utilisation of assets transferred out of the incumbent class RISES in framework-qualifying cases, in contrast to their general finding that liquidation lowers utilisation.

Substrate/overlay split: within any overbuild, assets with a high ratio of long-lived immobile substrate cost to short-lived programmable overlay cost will be the ones that transfer and appreciate in use; low-ratio assets will be scrapped. Applied to the AI buildout this predicts grid interconnects, substations and datacentre shells transfer and hold value while GPU fleets are written off — and that the eventual L3 entrants are firms holding power and buildings, not firms holding 2024-vintage silicon.

Kermani–Ma magnitude test: the price at which bust-era capacity changes hands should be predicted overwhelmingly by pre-bust physical attributes (mobility, durability, customisation) and only marginally (≤10pp) by bust severity. If bust severity dominates, the section-4 restatement is wrong and the original 'bubble makes it cheap' claim is rehabilitated.

Reset persistence: L3 cost-basis advantage should decay to zero within one asset replacement cycle in any case where real replacement cost of the capacity deflates faster than ~5%/yr. This predicts semiconductor fabs and GPU fleets never generate durable L3 advantage from bust-era acquisition, while trenched conduit, rights-of-way and grid interconnection rights do.

theory.analysis:
## 1. What Chapter 11 actually did in US telecom — the claim moved, not the fibre

The Cogent datum is real but atypical, and it has been over-read. In the large US telecom cases the physical asset did not change hands at all; the *capital structure* was rewritten around a stationary asset. WorldCom filed July 2002 with $103.9bn of assets, then the largest US bankruptcy ever. Global Crossing filed 28 January 2002 listing $22.44bn assets against $12.39bn debts, and emerged 9 December 2003 with ST Telemedia taking 61.5% for $250m — creditors took the remaining 38.5% in equity. NTL converted $10.6bn of debt to equity (a larger default than Enron's $9.9bn), cutting interest by roughly $850m/year. In none of these did a strand of glass move. What moved was the discount rate at which the capacity could be priced: once the debt claim is extinguished, the operator prices toward marginal cost, and that is what the L3 buys. Cogent's 0.4-cents-on-the-dollar acquisitions are the visible extreme of a mechanism whose main channel is invisible — **loss recognition, not title transfer**.

This matters because it identifies the correct ex-ante observable, which is not the insolvency statute but **who holds the claim and at what accounting basis**. US telecom was bondholder-financed: telecom was roughly a third of the Barclays US High Yield Index by 2000, and telecom accounted for 55% of 2001 high-yield defaults and 52% of 2002 (Altman). Bondholders are dispersed, marked to market, hold no regulatory capital against the position, and have no relationship rent to protect. That is the true differentiator from Japan, where the identical exposure sat with undercapitalised banks carrying loans at book.

## 2. NextWave vs Germany — the cleanest legal experiment available

*FCC v. NextWave Personal Communications*, 537 U.S. 293 (2003), 8–1: §525 of the Bankruptcy Code bars a regulator from cancelling a licence for non-payment of a debt dischargeable in bankruptcy. NextWave had bid ~$4.7bn in 1996, defaulted, and filed in June 1998; the FCC had cancelled. After the ruling, the spectrum moved through the bankruptcy court — Cingular bought 34 PCS licences for $1.4bn (approved September 2003), Verizon and MetroPCS took three more for roughly $1bn, and NextWave emerged in 2005.

Germany is the control. MobilCom and Quam (the Telefónica/Sonera JV) *returned* their UMTS licences with no refund after failing coverage obligations; Sonera wrote off €4.2bn. The returned spectrum was not re-auctioned until **May 2010** — eight years fallow. Same shock, same asset class, opposite institutional outcome: in the US, bankruptcy law dominated spectrum policy; in Germany, spectrum policy dominated insolvency and the asset was legally *unable* to transfer. This is the operator's reframing in its strongest form, and it is observable ex ante by reading the licence terms.

## 3. Japan — the framing is wrong, but the finding survives inverted

Three corrections to the assignment's premise.

**(a) Japan's insolvency law was not the problem.** The Civil Rehabilitation Act took effect 1 April 2000 — a DIP procedure explicitly modelled on Chapter 11 logic, with ~1,300 filings by September 2001 and court time cut from 12–14 months to about five. The Corporate Reorganization Law reform took effect 1 April 2003. Japan scores 92.1 cents recovery in *Doing Business 2020*, among the best in the world — better than the United States. A framework that says "bad bankruptcy law → no L3" is falsified by Japan on its own terms.

**(b) The choke point was creditor loss recognition, and it was released administratively, not judicially.** Peek & Rosengren (2005) show evergreening concentrated in banks near the minimum capital ratio; Caballero, Hoshi & Kashyap note that proper classification would have forced ~70% provisioning. The unblocking event was Takenaka's Program for Financial Revival (October 2002), Resona's nationalisation (2003) and the IRCJ (April 2003); major-bank NPL ratios fell to 2.9% by March 2005. So the binding institution was **supervisory forbearance policy**, not bankruptcy procedure — a different, and separately observable, variable.

**(c) Japan did get L3s, through three non-bankruptcy transfer channels.** Softbank's Yahoo!BB launched September 2001 at ¥990/month for 8Mbps over *unbundled NTT copper*, taking Japan to the world's cheapest DSL — mandated third-party access achieved what a fire sale achieves, with no title transfer whatever. J-REITs were enabled by the November 2000 amendment to the Investment Trust Act, first two listings 10 September 2001 at ~¥260bn combined, reaching ~¥6.7trn by May 2007 — the overbuilt property stock transferred to different people via *securities law*. And in manufacturing, Caballero et al. explicitly attribute the low zombie share to global competition and to troubled automakers being taken over by foreign firms rather than rescued — **cross-border control acquisition** as the disciplining device.

The CHK magnitudes still bear on the framework and are strong: ~30% of listed firms on bank life support in the early 2000s; asset-weighted zombie index rising 3.11%→9.58% in manufacturing (1981–93 vs 1996–2002) but 4.47%→20.35% in construction; cumulative lost investment for the median non-zombie wholesaler of 43.2% of capital (lower bound 17%, i.e. over a year's investment); real-estate non-zombie employment growth 9.5pp lower. Their footnote 24 is the decisive control the programme should adopt: running the same specification on US Compustat 1995–2004, the congestion coefficient is **insignificantly different from zero**. The US did not have a zombie problem in exactly the telecom-bust window.

But Fukao & Kwon complicate it fatally for a naive "no transfer" story: Japan's *exit effect was negative* — productive small firms were liquidated by the credit crunch while insolvent large borrowers were kept alive. Title transferred; it transferred adversely selected. The variable is not the speed of transfer but its **selection**.

## 4. Europe post-3G — two-tier, and the tier that failed produced the L3

Incumbents were rescued: France Télécom carried €68.0bn net debt at end-2002 and received a €9bn state credit line the Commission later ruled unlawful aid (decision of 2 August 2004). Sector market capitalisation fell 67% from $1.02trn to $630bn between January 2000 and July 2003, and Europe's share of cumulative global TMT market cap collapsed from 30% to 7% (McKinsey).

Yet the *altnets* did go through insolvency, and they did produce an L3. KPNQwest was declared bankrupt in the Netherlands on 31 May 2002; the 10,000km Ebone segment was physically shut down on 3 July 2002 after the Belgian administrator rejected a €15m bid; Interoute then bought the principal Ebone assets from the Irish receivers for about €15m against a build cost near €1bn. Interoute was sold to GTT in 2018 for $2.3bn / €1.9bn — a European Cogent, 126x, on the same clock. And NTL, a *British* cable network, restructured under *US* Chapter 11 because the parent was a Delaware corporation; NTL plus Telewest became Virgin Media. The UK's principal broadband L3 was manufactured by American bankruptcy law applied to British assets. That is a within-country forum experiment, and it favours the reframing.

Where Europe genuinely did not reset — incumbent-held towers and access networks — the L3 arrived roughly fifteen years late and by a different instrument: Cellnex spun out of Abertis Telecom in 2015 and consolidated European towers at 15–20x EBITDA, driven by incumbent deleveraging rather than default. Same direction, slower clock.

## 5. The disconfirming case the framework must carry: US airlines

Chapter 11 is not uniformly reallocative. In US airlines the standard complaint from solvent carriers is that Chapter 11 *preserved* overcapacity — the domestic zombie-carrier problem — and Borenstein & Rose (1995) find only patchy fare effects (Eastern and TWA cut fares; Continental and America West did not) with rivals' fares ending about 1% above pre-filing levels. The asymmetry that reconciles this: in telecom the written-down asset was a **general-purpose input to a different downstream industry** (cheap transit does not hurt Amazon, it creates Amazon), whereas in airlines it was **competing output capacity in the same market**, with no downstream L3 to feed. The legal regime is therefore a conditional enabler operating only on assets that already have general-purpose input character.

## 6. Two further confounds

Shleifer–Vishny fire-sale logic says the 0.4-cent price is itself a measure of the *absence* of solvent industry buyers — asset illiquidity, not good allocation. And Djankov, Hart, McLiesh & Shleifer (2008) show going-concern preservation versus piecemeal sale is strongly correlated with per-capita income and legal origin, so "fast title transfer" is badly confounded with development level and cannot be used as an independent variable in a broad cross-country panel. Finally, an unexamined live falsifier: China's fibre/solar/EV/property overbuild has produced world-beating downstream firms while title conspicuously does *not* transfer (the January 2024 Hong Kong liquidation order against Evergrande being largely unenforceable onshore). If price collapse via state-tolerated below-cost competition delivers the same cheap L2 input without any loss recognition, the reframing needs to be stated at the level of *input price*, not *legal title*.
theory.headline_finding: The premise of the assignment is itself wrong in a way that matters more than the answer. Cogent's $14bn-for-$60m was not produced by a *liquidating* regime — Chapter 11 is a reorganising regime, and in the large US telecom cases (WorldCom, $103.9bn assets; Global Crossing, $22.44bn assets sold 61.5% to ST Telemedia for $250m; NTL, $10.6bn debt-for-equity) the fibre never moved: the claim was extinguished while the asset stayed put. Meanwhile the European case that most closely resembles true liquidation — KPNQwest's Dutch bankruptcy, where the Ebone network was physically switched off on 3 July 2002 before sale — nonetheless produced a textbook L3: Interoute bought the assets for about €15m against a €1bn build cost and sold to GTT in 2018 for $2.3bn. And Japan, the supposed no-transfer control, had a Chapter-11-style DIP statute in force from 1 April 2000 and ranks near the top of the world on statutory insolvency efficiency (92.1 cents recovery, Doing Business 2020) — better than the United States — while still producing three separate L3s through non-bankruptcy channels: mandated local-loop unbundling (Yahoo!BB, ¥990/month for 8Mbps from September 2001, giving Japan the world's cheapest DSL), a securitisation vehicle (J-REITs, enabled November 2000, ¥260bn in 2001 to ~¥6.7trn by May 2007), and cross-border control acquisition in manufacturing. The operative institution is therefore not bankruptcy and not title transfer; it is **forced recognition of loss on the L2 capital, plus transfer of operating control to agents with no sunk commitment to the L1/L2 model**, of which liquidating bankruptcy is only one of at least four instruments.
theory.implications_for_framework: This QUALIFIES the framework sharply and reframes its enabling condition — it does not break it, but it destroys the version of it the operator currently holds. Three consequences. (1) Replace "bankruptcy regime" with a two-part condition that is genuinely observable ex ante: (i) is the L2 capital carried at a basis that will be forcibly written down, and (ii) is operating control transferable to agents with no sunk commitment to the L1/L2 model? The correct ex-ante diagnostic is a *creditor-structure and accounting* question, not a statute question — US telecom debt was bondholder-held, marked to market, ~a third of the high-yield index, with no regulatory capital at stake; Japanese exposure sat with undercapitalised banks at book with the minimum capital ratio binding (Peek & Rosengren). Japan's blockage was released administratively (Takenaka's Program for Financial Revival, October 2002; Resona 2003; IRCJ April 2003; major-bank NPLs to 2.9% by March 2005), not judicially. (2) The framework must carry a bounding condition it currently lacks: reorganisation bankruptcy is reallocative only when the written-down asset is a general-purpose input to a *different* downstream industry. Where it is competing output capacity in the same market, Chapter 11 manufactures zombies functionally identical to Japanese bank forbearance — US airlines are the standing counterexample, and the "zombie carrier" complaint is the domestic mirror of Caballero-Hoshi-Kashyap. (3) The strongest single piece of ex-ante-observable evidence in the whole programme is now the NextWave/Germany pair: FCC v. NextWave (537 U.S. 293, 2003, 8–1) subordinated spectrum policy to §525 of the Bankruptcy Code and the licences moved to Cingular ($1.4bn for 34) and Verizon within eighteen months, while MobilCom's and Quam's German UMTS licences were surrendered without refund and left fallow until the May 2010 re-auction. That is a clean, pre-registrable test on a legal document, and it should replace Cogent as the programme's headline datum. Caveats that must be carried: Shleifer–Vishny implies the fire-sale price measures asset illiquidity rather than allocative quality; Djankov-Hart-McLiesh-Shleifer show going-concern preservation is heavily confounded with income level and legal origin, so this cannot be run as an independent variable in a broad country panel; Fukao & Kwon show Japan's exit effect was *negative* (productive SMEs died, zombies lived), so the variable is selection of transfer, not speed; and China's post-2015 overbuild — where downstream champions emerged with essentially no loss recognition and no title transfer — is an unexamined live falsifier that should be the next agent's assignment.

testable_propositions: The L3 lag from an overbuild episode is decreasing in the share of L2 capital financed by mark-to-market instruments (public bonds, securitised debt) and increasing in the share held by prudentially regulated banks at amortised cost. Measurable ex ante from the financing mix at the peak of the frenzy; predicts US telecom 2001 (fast) vs Japan 1990 (slow) vs European incumbents 2002 (slow) without reference to any bankruptcy statute.

Where overbuilt capacity is licensed rather than owned and the licence is not transferable in insolvency, no L3 emerges from that capacity within ten years; it lies fallow until administratively reallocated. Confirmed by German UMTS (surrendered 2002, re-auctioned May 2010) against NextWave (Supreme Court January 2003, licences resold to Cingular and Verizon 2003-05). Falsified by any case of a non-transferable licensed asset generating an L3 inside a decade.

Reorganisation bankruptcy produces an L3 only when the written-down asset is a general-purpose input to a DIFFERENT downstream industry. Where it is competing output capacity in the same product market, Chapter 11 produces congestion statistically indistinguishable from Japanese bank forbearance. Test: run the Caballero-Hoshi-Kashyap congestion specification on US airlines 1990-2010; the coefficient should be significantly negative, unlike the near-zero the authors report for US Compustat 1995-2004 (their fn. 24).

Within a single jurisdiction and a single overbuild, firms resolved in a going-concern-preserving forum supply L3 entrants sooner and cheaper than identically situated firms resolved in a piecemeal forum. Test: NTL (UK cable, US Chapter 11 via Delaware incorporation, reorganised 2002-03, becomes Virgin Media) against KPNQwest (Dutch faillissement, network dark 3 July 2002, assets to Interoute). Predicts a two-to-four-year delay in L3 service availability on the piecemeal path, and it should be visible in European transit and IP-VPN pricing 2002-06.

If loss recognition rather than title transfer is the operative mechanism, jurisdictions that force write-downs administratively with no insolvency proceeding should show reallocation resuming within roughly three years. Test on Japan: the Program for Financial Revival (October 2002), Resona nationalisation (2003) and IRCJ (April 2003) should be followed by a break in the zombie capital share, the exit effect, and reallocation-driven TFP growth in 2004-07 — and by the FIRST post-bubble Japanese L3 entries in the previously zombified non-tradable sectors (retail, construction, real estate).

Caballero-Hoshi-Kashyap's congestion coefficient should be near zero in Japanese manufacturing and significantly negative in Japanese construction, real estate and services over 1996-2002, because manufacturing's discipline came from foreign product-market competition and foreign control acquisition rather than from insolvency. This isolates control transfer, not legal title, as the mechanism and can be tested directly on their published sample.

Where insolvency is blocked but MANDATED THIRD-PARTY ACCESS to the overbuilt asset is imposed, an L3 emerges on a comparable clock to the bankruptcy path. Test: Japanese DSL after NTT local-loop unbundling (Yahoo!BB, September 2001) should show entry timing and input-price collapse comparable to post-Chapter-11 US transit pricing over 2001-05, despite zero change in asset ownership.

FALSIFIER, currently untested: China's post-2015 solar, EV, battery, fibre and property overbuild produced dominant downstream firms with essentially no loss recognition and no title transfer (the Hong Kong liquidation order against Evergrande, January 2024, being largely unenforceable onshore). If confirmed, the enabling condition must be restated at the level of realised INPUT PRICE rather than legal title or loss recognition — i.e. any institution that forces L2 capacity to be sold below its embedded capital cost will do, including state-tolerated below-cost competition.

theory.headline_finding: The shakeout literature contradicts the operator's framework on two counts, not one — and the second is worse than the "who captures value" problem the assignment anticipated. First, on identity: across the four industries Klepper and Simons built firm-by-firm datasets for (autos, tyres, TV receivers, penicillin), the post-shakeout oligopolists are early entrants, adjacent-industry diversifiers, or spinoffs of the best early entrants — 4 out of 4, with no de novo post-peak cohort capturing leadership in any of them. In US autos, 725 firms entered 1895–1966, producers peaked at 272 in 1909 and fell to 9 by 1941; at age 15 the 1895–1904 cohort's annual exit hazard was 76% below the 1910–66 cohort's, rising to 90% by age 25 (Klepper 2001/2002). GM, Ford and Chrysler all descend genealogically from four early Detroit entrants — Olds, Buick, Cadillac, Ford — which spawned 22 spinoffs and 41 total descendants; Walter Chrysler was ex-president of Buick, Charles Nash ex-president of GM. In television, prior radio producers were only about a fifth of entrants but almost every top radio maker entered and they dominated both survival and share — Klepper and Simons literally titled it "dominance by birthright." Second, and more damaging: Klepper's shakeout is not caused by an L2 shock at all. He and Simons show explicitly that shakeouts are not triggered by particular innovations or by dominant designs; the cull is endogenous, generated by returns to process R&D scaling with output so that early, high-R&D-productivity firms compound an advantage. The assignment framed Klepper as a measured base rate *for* L2. He is closer to evidence that L2-as-discrete-shock is unnecessary: the modal technologically progressive industry reorganises and culls 90%+ of its producers with no bubble, no malinvestment and no forced restructuring anywhere in the causal chain.
theory.analysis:
## 1. What the literature actually measures, and against what unit

Gort and Klepper (1982, Economic Journal 92: 630–653) hand-counted producers for 46 new products from trade volumes and fitted a five-stage path: commercialisation, sharp rise in producer numbers, shakeout, stabilisation, maturity. This is the only large-N multi-industry dataset in which innovations are counted directly from primary sources rather than proxied by patents. Two of its numbers matter here. Stage I duration fell from 23.1 years for products introduced before 1930 to 4.9 years for those after 1940 (secondary summary; I could not open the original PDF). And patents rise over the life cycle while *major* innovations fall — the opposite of the naive reading.

Klepper (1996, AER 86: 562–583) supplies the formal engine. Firms differ in R&D productivity a_i. Total rents from process R&D equal the cost reduction times output, so returns scale with firm size; larger and earlier firms therefore invest more, cut costs more, and expand faster. Price-cost margins fall, the minimum a_i needed to enter profitably rises, entry ceases, and the lowest-productivity late entrants exit first. Concentration and shakeout are joint outputs of the same process. Crucially the advantage is *firm-embodied and non-tradeable* — a_i is a parameter of the organisation. The only transfer channel Klepper ever admits is heredity: employees leaving to found spinoffs.

Klepper (2001, "The Evolution of the U.S. Automobile Industry and Detroit as Its Capital") gives the cleanest quantitative base rate available. 725 entrants (219 in 1895–1904, 271 in 1905–09, 235 in 1910–66). Entry peaked at 82 firms in 1907; producers peaked at 272 in 1909 and bottomed at 9 in 1941 — a 96.7% cull over 32 years. Entrant composition: 120 experienced diversifiers, 108 experienced entrepreneurs, 145 spinoffs, 352 inexperienced. Hazard estimates: at age 15, cohorts 1 and 2 had annual hazards 76% and 48% below cohort 3; at age 25, 90% and 67% below. A Detroit-location dummy showed a 25% lower hazard — and went insignificant once spinoff heritage was controlled. Klepper's conclusion is unambiguous: pedigree, not place. Only 15% of all entrants located in Detroit, but 37% of all *spinoffs* did; Detroit spinoffs' parents had produced ten-plus years in 66% of cases versus 48% elsewhere. Tellingly, no inexperienced Detroit firm survived past ten years.

Tyres peaked at roughly 278 producers in 1922 (up from 157 in 1917); TV receivers at roughly 95 in 1950, falling to 35 by 1960 and 20 by 1970 (both figures secondary — treat as approximate).

## 2. How often is it a new cohort?

At the level of the *product market*, essentially never in the measured sample. Autos: 0/3 leaders unconnected to the early cohort. TV: radio incumbents. Tyres: early-entering Akron firms and their spinoffs. Penicillin: the pharmaceutical incumbents that scaled wartime fermentation. Lasers: Klepper's own anomaly — no shakeout for 35 years — resolved by Bhaskarabhatla and Klepper (2014, ICC 23: 1381–1415), who show that laser submarkets were non-substitutable (different wavelengths, powers), so no single submarket was large enough to induce R&D escalation; atomistic structure and profitable entry persisted for decades until the diode-pumped solid-state laser *fused* previously separate submarkets and the shakeout arrived on schedule.

The one large-N result that cuts the operator's way is Golder and Tellis (1993, JMR 30: 158–170): ~500 brands across 50 categories; pioneer failure rate 47% versus 8% for early followers; surviving pioneers hold ~10% share against ~28% for early market leaders, who enter on average 13 years after the pioneer. That is a measured cohort discontinuity with a measured lag — the operator's strongest empirical asset in this literature. But note the lag is 13 years, not "decades," and Klepper would classify most of those early leaders as *early entrants with superior capabilities*, not as a third generation.

Chandy and Tellis (2000, Journal of Marketing 64: 1–17) is the decisive temporal qualifier. Of 64 radical innovations with complete data, 53% came from non-incumbents and 47% from incumbents — not significantly different. Split by era: pre-WWII, 73% non-incumbent and 83% small/medium firms; post-WWII, 74% incumbent and 74% large firms. The "outsiders bring the radical stuff" regularity is a pre-1945 phenomenon in their sample. Tushman and Anderson (1986, ASQ 31: 439–465) supply the standard discriminator — competence-destroying discontinuities are initiated by entrants, competence-enhancing by incumbents — but King and Tucci (2002, Management Science 48: 171–186) re-ran the disk-drive data and found that incumbents with more prior entry and production experience were *more* likely to enter new niches and did well there, a direct partial rebuttal of the Christensen reading.

On the finance side, the Marathon/Chancellor capital cycle says the same thing as Klepper by a different route: capital exits, supply shrinks, survivors earn excess returns. Marathon's own recorded failures are the informative part — they lost where supply-side consolidation was swamped by secular demand decline or business-model displacement. That is the boundary condition stated by practitioners, in the operator's own vocabulary.

## 3. What actually distinguishes the exceptions

Four discriminators, ranked by how well the literature supports them.

**(a) Asset alienability.** Klepper's advantage is a firm-level parameter that cannot be bought. The operator's canonical L2 assets — dark fibre, fabs, rolling stock, empty datacentre shells — are *alienable at distress prices*. When the L2 overbuild is embodied in tradeable capital, the buyer's identity is unconstrained by heredity, and a new cohort becomes possible. When it is embodied in routines, R&D productivity, dealer networks or tacit process knowledge, only survivors and their spinoffs can hold it. This is the real difference between fibre in 2002 and Akron in 1922, and it is not a discriminator anyone in the shakeout literature has formalised, because Klepper's model has no secondhand asset market at all.

**(b) Submarket boundary crossing.** Klepper and Thompson (2006, RAND 37: 861–886) make growth and survival a function of capturing new submarkets. Bhaskarabhatla and Klepper show submarket *proliferation* suppresses shakeout and leaves room for entrants for decades; submarket *fusion* triggers shakeout and survivor capture. Value moves to a new cohort when it accrues in a submarket the incumbent's capability does not reach.

**(c) Shared-asset conflict.** Bresnahan, Greenstein and Henderson (2011, NBER ch. 12354) is the most precise ex-ante test available. IBM in PCs and Microsoft in browsers both succeeded initially via autonomous units and then failed when the new business had to share firm-level assets with the old on incompatible terms; control reverted to the old business and crippled the new. Not cannibalisation, not cognitive framing — diseconomies of scope in shared assets. You can ask, before the fact, which asset must be shared.

**(d) Architectural layer.** Bresnahan and Greenstein (1999, JIE 47: 1–40) describe indirect entry across segment boundaries and vertical disintegration producing divided technical leadership. Jacobides, Knudsen and Augier (2006, Research Policy 35) formalise who captures value as a function of industry architecture and bottleneck position rather than of who innovated.

## 4. The problem this creates for the framework

Apply the discriminators to the operator's own canonical cases and both partly fail. Case (b): AWS is Amazon (founded 1994, IPO 1997 — a frenzy-era firm that survived); Azure is Microsoft, an L1/L2 incumbent; Netflix was founded 1997; Google 1998. Round 1 already established Cogent (1999) and Internap (1996) as bubble-era firms. Only Cloudflare (2009) is a clean post-crash founding. The dot-com/fibre case is dominated by *bubble-era survivors buying distressed capacity* — Klepper plus Marathon, not a third generation. Case (a): Ford Motor entered in 1903 and Henry Ford had been in Detroit vehicles since 1899; GM's components Buick, Cadillac and Olds date to 1903, 1902 and 1901. Relative to the automobile industry these are first-cohort firms. They read as "different people" only when the reference frame is *electrification*, in which case they are a different industry by construction.

That is the point that matters. Round 1 established that the ordinal L1/L2/L3 is indexical to where the analyst starts counting. The "different people" feature is not an independent, testable addition to the framework — it is *entailed* by the layer assignment. Widen the frame and the winners are always different people; narrow it to the product market and they are always the same lineage. Adding the cohort-discontinuity claim does not increase falsifiability; it re-encodes the same free parameter.
theory.implications_for_framework: Qualifies severely, and breaks one specific component. (1) The "different people" feature must be demoted from a claimed regularity to a *conditional* outcome, because the only measured base rate — Klepper's four industries, plus lasers — runs 4/4 the other way, and the effect sizes are large (early-cohort hazards 76–90% lower at ages 15–25). (2) The feature is not independently falsifiable: whether the L3 cohort is "different people" is determined by the industry boundary the analyst chose when assigning layers, which round 1 already showed is free. Do not treat it as a second, corroborating test of the framework — it is the same free parameter wearing a different hat. (3) The framework's causal story for L2 is unsupported: Klepper and Simons show shakeouts are not triggered by dominant designs or discrete technological events, so a bubble/malinvestment L2 is not necessary for the reorganisation-then-oligopoly pattern. If the operator wants L2 to be doing causal work, he must specify what the bubble adds beyond the endogenous R&D-escalation mechanism that produces the same outcome without one. (4) The framework survives, in restricted form, only where the L2 overbuild leaves behind *alienable* capacity — tradeable physical assets or mobile trained labour — that is most valuable in a different product market or architectural layer than the one financed to build it. That is the exception class, and it is the one thing here worth keeping. Recommended reframe: stop claiming "different people" and claim "different firms, same lineage, unless the L2 asset is alienable and the value migrates across a submarket boundary." Klepper's spinoff/heredity results make the human-capital continuity explicit — his answer to "where do the new people come from" is "the best incumbents' payrolls."

testable_propositions: Conditional on a product market experiencing a Gort-Klepper shakeout (peak-to-trough producer decline exceeding 50%), the post-shakeout top three by share will contain zero firms founded de novo after the producer-count peak year, in at least 80% of cases. Autos, tyres, TV receivers and penicillin are 4/4 consistent; the operator's 45-case corpus should be re-scored on this rule.

Where the L2 overbuild is embodied in ALIENABLE assets traded in distress at under ~20% of replacement cost, the probability that a post-peak founding reaches the post-shakeout top three is materially above zero; where the L2 capability is firm-embodied (process R&D productivity, distribution, tacit routines), it is approximately zero. This is the single discriminating variable and it is absent from Klepper's model, which has no secondhand asset market.

First-cohort entrants have annual exit hazards 70-90% below last-cohort entrants at ages 15-25 (Klepper, autos). Any framework predicting that a late cohort captures value must specify the mechanism by which this hazard ordering reverses, and name the case in which it has been observed to reverse.

The median lag between pioneer entry and entry of the eventual long-run share leader is ~13 years within a product category (Golder & Tellis). The operator's 'decades' is roughly 2-3x too long if the unit is a product market, and defensible only if the unit is a sector spanning multiple product markets — which forces the layer-assignment problem back into the open.

Gort-Klepper Stage I duration fell from 23.1 years (pre-1930 products) to 4.9 years (post-1940). If the operator's lag is structural, it must be shrinking on the same trend. A framework asserting a constant multi-decade lag is falsified by this time series.

Post-1945, ~74% of radical innovations come from incumbents and ~74% from large firms (Chandy & Tellis). Any claim that L1-to-L3 transitions are normally executed by outsiders is a pre-1945 regularity and should not be extrapolated forward without a stated reason.

Bresnahan-Greenstein-Henderson shared-asset test, stated ex ante: incumbents fail to capture L3 if and only if the L3 business requires shared use of a firm-level asset with the L1/L2 business on incompatible terms. Name the shared asset before the outcome is known; if no such asset exists, predict incumbent capture.

Bhaskarabhatla-Klepper submarket test: shakeout timing is predicted by the arrival of a technology that renders previously non-substitutable submarkets substitutable. Absent such fusion, no shakeout occurs and atomistic structure persists (US lasers: 35 years). A framework predicting an inevitable L2 cull must specify why submarket fusion is guaranteed.

The 'different people' claim is not separately falsifiable: for any case, there exists a choice of industry boundary that makes the L3 winners a new cohort and another that makes them the L1 cohort's lineal descendants. Test by pre-registering the boundary (SIC/NAICS level, or the product-market definition Gort used) before scoring cohort identity. If scoring flips under reasonable boundary choices, drop the feature.

theory.headline_finding: Four of the nine literatures contradict the framework, and the two the operator hoped would rescue it are the two that damage it most. (i) Farmer & Lafond (2016) is real forecastability but of the wrong variable: it predicts the unit cost of an already-named artefact, not which artefact or who sells it — and it works precisely because cost curves are smooth difference-stationary random walks with drift, i.e. the absence of the discontinuous layer-jump the cascade requires. It is also mis-cited: F&L 2016 fit a time-based (Moore) model to 53 technologies; the Wright-vs-Moore horse race is Nagy, Farmer, Bui & Trancik (2013, 62 technologies), and Wright and Moore finished roughly tied, with Sahal's conjecture confirmed (when production grows exponentially the two laws are observationally near-identical). (ii) Product space is worse news still: Li & Neffke (2023), searching tens of thousands of specifications on US city-industry data, find relatedness predicts where industries *are* far better than where they *grow* — among city-industries with the most negative residuals (the framework's "adjacent possible" candidates), the growth-spurt rate is 3.36% against a 2.68% base rate. Relatedness is a screening-out instrument, not a picking instrument. (iii) Aglietta inverts the canonical example (a)'s sequence: the Fordist transformation of the labour process long preceded any rise in working-class consumption; Fordism-as-regime was an institutional settlement won by 1930s–40s labour struggle and collective bargaining, not a technological consequence — and Gramsci named it contemporaneously in 1929–30, so the "decades of lag before anyone sees it" claim fails for the operator's own flagship case. (iv) Goldfarb, Kirsch & Miller (2007) find *too little* entry in the Dot Com era, not overbuild: five-year dot-com survival approached 50%, at or above other emerging industries in their formative years, and survival was unrelated to receipt or amount of private equity.
theory.analysis:
**(1) FORDISM — names L3 of example (a), but reassigns its causal content from technology to institutions.**

Gramsci coined the analytic use of "Fordism" in *Americanism and Fordism* (Prison Notebooks, composed c.1929–30). His claims are sharper than the operator's: high wages are a *transitory* form of remuneration tied to a temporary monopoly of new methods, and disappear once the discipline is internalised; hegemony "is born in the factory"; the precondition was America's lack of parasitic rentier strata consuming surplus value. Note the timing — the third order was named while it was happening.

Aglietta's *Régulation et crises du capitalisme* (1976; Eng. *A Theory of Capitalist Regulation*, 1979) supplies the machinery: **regime of accumulation** (the pattern of surplus-value extraction, extensive vs intensive, spanning both labour process and the modes of social reproduction/working-class consumption outside the workplace) and **mode of regulation** (the articulation of *structural forms* — collective bargaining, credit, monetary norms — that let a regime stabilise). He periodises US capitalism into five phases; Fordism emerges from the 1919–45 crises. The decisive correction, as Durand's NLR obituary (2025) restates: the labour-process transformation long preceded rising working-class consumption. Collective bargaining, healthcare plans and pension funds — not the assembly line — made Fordism a *regime*, by covering social reproduction and channelling contractual savings into credit that financed the "car and a house" consumption norm. Fordism then generated its own contradictions (inflation replacing unemployment as the adjustment valve; physical limits to line speed-up; wildcat strikes) and entered generalised crisis from 1966.

So: the Regulation School names the operator's L3 but denies that L3 is a *downstream* effect of L1/L2. It is a co-equal political settlement whose failure modes are endogenous. Boyer's and Lipietz's extensions (peripheral Fordism, the crisis of the wage relation) preserve this: crises are crises of the *mode of regulation*, not of the technology.

Piore & Sabel, *The Second Industrial Divide* (1984), do something the framework should adopt wholesale: they treat mass production not as the inevitable third order but as the winner of a **contingent branching point** — an "industrial divide" at which craft/flexible-specialisation paths were genuinely available and lost politically, not technically. This is the single most damaging idea here for a deterministic cascade, and the most useful one for a probabilistic version: it converts "L3 emerges" into "one of several L3s is selected."

**(2) GENERATIVITY (Zittrain 2008) — names the L1/L2→L3 *unpredictability property*, and supplies the framework's only intrinsic stopping rule.**

Definition: a system's capacity to produce unanticipated change through unfiltered contributions from broad and varied audiences. Five factors: leverage, adaptability, ease of mastery, accessibility, transferability. Crucially these are assessable *ex ante* on a substrate, so generativity escapes circularity: you cannot predict which L3 appears, but you can rank candidate L2 substrates by expected L3 diversity. The hourglass/procrastination-principle argument explains the mechanism — a deliberately feature-poor narrow waist (IP) pushes problem-solving up and down to others, which is *why* the substrate's builders are not the L3 winners.

The under-used part is Zittrain's **generative pattern as lifecycle**: generative success invites abuse, which invites appliancisation and tethering, which destroys generativity. This predicts that L3 winners close the substrate and foreclose L4 — an endogenous terminus for the layer count, which speaks directly to round 1's indexicality problem. The ordinal need not recurse forever if generativity decays.

**(3) DOMINANT DESIGN / ERA OF FERMENT — names the internal structure of L2, and decomposes "value."**

Utterback & Abernathy (1975, *Omega* 3:639–56): fluid → transitional → specific phases, with dominant design at the transition. Anderson & Tushman (1990, *ASQ* 35(4)) formalise the cycle — discontinuity → era of ferment (design competition and substitution) → dominant design → era of incremental change — on cement, glass and minicomputers. Two findings matter. First, **eras of ferment account for the majority of observed technical progress**, yet **sales always peak after a dominant design emerges**. That is a clean decomposition: technical progress in L2, value capture in L3 — which supports the operator's value-capture claim while destroying any reading of L2 as wasteful. Second, both the *length* of the ferment and *which type of firm* sets the standard are contingent on how the discontinuity hits existing competences.

That contingency is Tushman & Anderson (1986, *ASQ* 31:439–65): discontinuities are **competence-enhancing** (initiated by incumbents) or **competence-destroying** (initiated by new entrants). This is the operator's "different people" feature stated as a *conditional*, with a pre-specifiable antecedent.

**(5) ABSORPTIVE CAPACITY (Cohen & Levinthal 1990, *ASQ* 35:128–52) — the missing mechanism, but it predicts the opposite of "different people" by default.**

Absorptive capacity is the ability to recognise the value of new external information, assimilate it, and apply it commercially; it is a function of prior related knowledge, is cumulative, path-dependent, domain-specific and largely non-transferable across fields, and arises as a by-product of own R&D (the "two faces of R&D"). Read straight, this says *incumbents* should exploit the residue best. The "different people" outcome therefore requires two extra conditions to hold jointly: the discontinuity is competence-destroying (T&A 1986), *and* the incumbent suffered **lockout** — failure to invest in absorptive capacity in a fast-moving field, which is not recoverable later. Combined, these turn a stylised fact into a falsifiable conditional and give the framework its first genuine ex ante discriminator.

**(6) VALUE MIGRATION.** Christensen & Raynor's **conservation of attractive profits**: when modularity and commoditisation destroy attractive profits at one stage, they reappear at an *adjacent* stage, wherever the not-good-enough performance bottleneck now sits, and the winning architecture there is interdependent/proprietary. As stated it inherits round 1's indexicality problem exactly — "adjacent" is undefined, so it narrates post hoc. Spolsky's **commoditise your complement** (Strategy Letter V, 2002) is the strictly better instrument because it is ex ante and behavioural: demand for a product rises when its complements' prices fall, so firms deliberately subsidise the layer they do not own (IBM opening the PC bus; Netscape giving away the browser; IBM funding Linux to sell services). This reframes L2 overbuild as *rational complement-commoditisation by identifiable actors with declared strategies*, not as anonymous malinvestment — and it is checkable against contemporaneous documents.

**(7) INFRASTRUCTURE AS COMMONS (Frischmann 2012).** Three criteria: partially non-rival; primary social value from enabling downstream productive activity; input into a *wide range* of outputs including private, public and non-market goods. The appropriation argument: because much downstream output is public/social goods with unmeterable value, a revenue-maximising owner discriminates toward observable high-willingness-to-pay commercial uses and systematically starves the low-appropriability, non-obvious uses that carry the largest social value. This gives a structural reason why L1/L2 owners cannot capture spillovers. But it cuts the operator too: in Frischmann's accounting the spillover is dissipated to *users*, not harvested by L3 firms. "L3 captures most of the value" is a claim about *private* value capture and must not be conflated with social value.

**(8) PRODUCT SPACE.** Hidalgo, Klinger, Barabási & Hausmann (2007, *Science* 317:482–87): countries move to goods proximate to what they already make; sophisticated goods sit in a dense core, and most poor countries can only reach it across empirically rare distances. Generalised as the **principle of relatedness** (Hidalgo et al. 2018) across products, industries, occupations and technologies. Mealy & Teytelboym (2022, *Research Policy* 51:103948) show the operational version — a green complexity ranking that predicts future green export growth and correlates with environmental patenting and lower emissions net of GDP. Two hard caveats. Mealy, Farmer & Teytelboym (2019, *Science Advances*) show ECI/PCI *are* a spectral clustering of the country-product bipartite graph — a dimensionality reduction, not a measurement of complexity. And Li & Neffke (2023) find 10–20% of relatedness specifications fail to beat random relatedness matrices, and the growth-spurt precision result above. Verdict: usable as an ex ante *feasibility filter* over candidate L3s given an L2 capability set; useless as a winner-picker.

**(9) COUNTER-LITERATURE.** Citation correction: there are two Rosenberg & Frischtak papers — "Long Waves and Economic Growth: A Critical Appraisal," *AER* P&P 73(2), 1983:146–51, and the full argument, "Technological Innovation and Long Waves," *Cambridge Journal of Economics* 8(1), 1984:7–24, reprinted as ch.4 of Rosenberg's *Exploring the Black Box*. At full strength they impose four requirements on any long-wave theory: **causality** (an exhaustively specified mechanism by which each phase produces the next, not mere sequence); **timing** (recurrence within precise bounds under stable causal relations); **economy-wide repercussions** (the innovation must plausibly move aggregate output, not one sector); and **recurrence** via an identified *endogenous* mechanism. Their charge is that no long-wave account meets them: innovations are not a homogeneous class that can be counted and clustered; causality plausibly runs from macroeconomic conditions *to* innovation rather than the reverse; and nothing explains why innovations should bunch at the trough. Their alternative is that observed variation may be a summation of random events. Goldfarb & Kirsch (*Bubbles and Crashes*, Stanford UP, 2019) do the empirical work: 58 technologies meeting their comparison criterion across ~150 years, a "frothiness" metric (standard deviations from predicted index trend over seven-year windows), and a four-factor account of when bubbles form — uncertainty about technological potential, susceptibility to positive narratives, novice investors, and pure plays. Most technologies do not bubble. Bubbles are a property of the *financing environment*, not of technological importance. Their bubble definition — investors driving up prices and getting fooled — is a claim about waste, and their earlier JFE paper supplies the mechanism: a "Get Big Fast" belief cascade among VCs, sustained by delayed feedback, that over-concentrated capital into too few internet startups.
theory.implications_for_framework: Qualify hard, and split the framework in two — because the two halves have opposite evidentiary standing. The **value-capture/organisational-succession half survives and can be strengthened into something falsifiable**: Tushman & Anderson's competence-destroying/competence-enhancing distinction plus Cohen & Levinthal's lockout gives a pre-specifiable antecedent for "different people"; Anderson & Tushman's finding that ferment carries most technical progress while sales peak after dominant design gives a clean progress/value decomposition; Frischmann explains why substrate owners structurally cannot appropriate; Spolsky explains why some of them deliberately don't try; Zittrain's five factors let you score a substrate ex ante for L3 diversity without naming the L3, and his generativity-decay lifecycle supplies an endogenous terminus that partially answers round 1's indexicality problem — the recursion stops when the winners appliancise the substrate. The **periodisation/bubble-necessity half should be abandoned or radically weakened.** Rosenberg & Frischtak's four requirements are not met by the cascade as stated (no endogenous recurrence mechanism, no specified timing bound, causality unestablished and plausibly reversed). Goldfarb & Kirsch show bubbles are a financing-environment phenomenon that most important technologies do not exhibit; Goldfarb, Kirsch & Miller show the canonical L2 — dot-com — was characterised by too *little* entry, ~50% five-year survival on par with or better than other emerging industries, and survival uncorrelated with VC funding. Combined with round 1's Cogent/Internap and Southwest corrections, the "productive bubble" leg is now the weakest part of the structure and should be demoted from mechanism to occasional accompaniment. On the prospective instrument question, the honest answer is that neither candidate delivers what was hoped. Farmer & Lafond genuinely forecast *cost of a specified artefact* with calibrated error bars, and that is a real, rare achievement — but it presupposes the artefact is already identified, forecasts nothing about application emergence, adoption, or value capture, and its own authors flag that structural breaks occur and that causal theories of *why* rates differ do not yet exist. Product space delivers an ex ante feasibility filter with a documented precision of 3.36% against a 2.68% base rate for growth spurts. Together they license a modest, defensible claim: **given a named L2 capability set and a named candidate L3 artefact, you can bound its cost trajectory and screen out infeasible adjacencies — you cannot pick the winner.** Finally, the Fordism material forces a substantive revision to example (a): the operator's own canonical case has an institutional, not technological, third order, whose sequence (labour process first, consumption norm second, via class conflict) inverts the cascade, and which Gramsci identified in real time. Either example (a) is retired as canonical, or the framework must admit political settlement as a first-class L3 generator — in which case Piore & Sabel's contingent industrial divide, not a determinate cascade, is the right ontology.
