testable_propositions: Competence-destroying condition: for cases where the L1/L2 discontinuity is coded ex ante as competence-destroying (per Tushman & Anderson 1986 criteria), L3 leaders will be new entrants in a significantly higher proportion than in competence-enhancing cases. If 'different people' occurs at similar rates in both, the framework's succession feature is not a technology-driven phenomenon.

Lockout condition: among incumbents who owned L1 or L2 assets, those who continued domain-specific R&D through the L2 phase will be over-represented among L3 winners relative to those who did not. If prior R&D confers no advantage, Cohen & Levinthal cannot be the mechanism and the 'different people' feature needs a different explanation (e.g. capital structure or sunk-cost commitment).

Generativity ranking: score candidate L2 substrates ex ante on Zittrain's five factors (leverage, adaptability, ease of mastery, accessibility, transferability). Higher-scoring substrates will yield a greater count and Herfindahl-diversity of distinct L3 application categories within a fixed window. This is predictable without predicting any individual L3.

Generativity decay / terminus: in cascades where L3 winners appliancise or tether the substrate (closed APIs, hardware attestation, vertical integration of the narrow waist), no L4 with comparable value capture will emerge from that substrate. This supplies a falsifiable stopping rule for the layer ordinal.

Cost-curve bound (Farmer-Lafond): for any named candidate L3 whose core input has >=10 years of unit-cost data, the L3's commercial viability threshold date can be forecast with calibrated error bars. Falsified if realised costs fall outside the 95% distributional interval more often than 5% of the time across a pre-registered set of cases.

Relatedness as filter, not picker: L3s that emerge will lie within a pre-specified proximity radius of the L2 capability set in product/technology space at rates well above chance; but among all candidates inside that radius, the hit rate will be only marginally above the base rate (Li & Neffke: 3.36% vs 2.68%). The framework may therefore claim exclusion power and must not claim selection power.

Bubble is not necessary (Goldfarb & Kirsch): across a pre-registered sample of L1 technologies, the presence of a frothiness episode in L2 will not predict the magnitude of L3 value capture. If most large L3 outcomes follow non-bubble L2 phases, 'productive bubble' must be demoted from mechanism to accompaniment.

Overbuild is not overentry: for any claimed L2 malinvestment phase, five-year survival rates of entrants will not be significantly below survival rates of entrants in matched emerging industries. Verified false for dot-com (~50%, at or above benchmark); test railway mania, telecom fibre, and any AI-era claim on the same standard.

Complement-commoditisation is deliberate: for cases coded as L2 overbuild, contemporaneous corporate documents will show identifiable actors publicly subsidising the layer they did not own for stated strategic reasons (Spolsky). If overbuild is instead anonymous and unstrategic, the malinvestment reading survives and the Spolsky reframing fails.

Institutional-settlement test (Aglietta/Piore-Sabel): in cascades where L3 involves a distributional or labour settlement, the settlement will be datable to organised political conflict rather than to technological capability arrival, and the labour-process change will precede the consumption-norm change. Verified for Fordism; test for post-war aviation, container shipping, and platform labour.

Rosenberg-Frischtak recurrence test: across the 45-case corpus, L1-to-L3 lag lengths will not cluster within stable bounds once the reference frame is fixed ex ante. If lags are dispersed and frame-dependent, the framework must be restated as a mechanism claim with no periodicity content.

stress.headline_finding: Example (a) breaks at three of its four joints, and the most damaging blow comes from the operator's own authorities rather than from any hostile source. David and Wright — the authors of the canonical electrification-lag literature the framework rests on — do not treat the assembly line as a downstream product of electrification at all. They describe "the technological confluence, or convergence, of electrification with other trajectories of industrial innovation, each of which might be considered a species of GPT" (David & Wright, *Early Twentieth Century Productivity Growth Dynamics*), and they explicitly note that automated materials handling "did not require electrification." That is a lattice of parallel converging trajectories, not a serial chain of derivatives. Concretely: Highland Park in 1913 ran on electric **group drive** — overhead line shafts each turned by a large DC motor, fed by Ford's own on-site gas-steam powerhouse — which is exactly the shallow, no-payoff configuration David and Devine identify as the phase in which motors were "merely added to the existing stock of equipment." The deep reorganisation (unit drive, single-storey linear layout) reached Ford in the **1920s**; Ford's own switch from multi-storey to single-storey branch plants dates to **1922**. So the moving line did not follow the shop-floor reorganisation; it sat between two phases of it and helped pull the second. Lindy Biggs: "Few machines ran on individual motors in the Ford factories even as late as 1918." Meanwhile the WWII tail should be cut outright: Alexander Field measures manufacturing TFP falling at −5.1% per year 1941–45.
stress.analysis:
## (1) The ordering problem at Ford — both horns bite

**What drive system did Highland Park use in 1913?** Electric group drive, not unit drive. Machines were arranged around overhead line shafts; each line shaft was turned by a large DC motor; the DC came from Ford's own coal-fired powerhouse on site (nine Ford-designed gas-steam hybrid engines, ~53,000 hp by 1919). This is panels B/C of Devine's taxonomy (electric line-shaft drive / electric group drive), not panel D (unit drive). Lindy Biggs, quoted in *Assembly* magazine's centennial piece: "Few machines ran on individual motors in the Ford factories even as late as 1918." The HAER report on Ford's Richmond plant independently confirms the constraint persisted: layout draftsman Max Wiesmyer joined Ford's Factory Layout Department in **1919**, and "configuring equipment with an eye to efficient connection to overhead line shafts was still an important parameter shaping design."

**Was Ford in the first decile of electrified plants?** In the sense that matters, yes — and it does not save the example. Highland Park (Kahn design 1908, built 1910) was 100% electrically driven at a date when electric motors supplied roughly a third of US manufacturing drive horsepower (~5% in 1900, ~25% in 1909, "just over 50 percent in 1919," "nearly 80 percent in 1929" — David & Wright, derived from DuBoff). So there is no literal ordering violation at the frontier. **I could not verify a first-decile claim rigorously**: the Census of Manufactures reported aggregate horsepower by drive type, not plant-level distributions, and no published decile ranking of 1913 plants exists that I could reach.

But the answer that saves the ordering destroys the causal structure. Ford was early on *shallow* electrification and late on *deep* electrification. The productivity payoff David and Devine identify comes from unit drive — which frees layout from the shaft, permits single-storey linear plants, and is what actually shows up in the numbers. At Ford that arrives in the 1920s, after the line. And the line's own ancestry is not electrical: William "Pa" Klann imported it from Chicago meatpacking disassembly; the enabling hardware was conveyors, gravity slides and overhead monorails.

Two further facts corrode the chain. First, **Ford self-generated**. Highland Park was an isolated plant, not a central-station customer, until Rouge power took over around 1926 — and Rouge was also Ford's own. The electric-utility industry is therefore not upstream of Ford in any supply sense. Second, the corrected sequence is: shallow electrification (1910) → moving line (1913) → unit drive + single-storey layout (1920s) → industrial TFP at ~5–6%/yr over 1919–29 versus roughly 1%/yr for 1899–1914. That is a genuine and quantified thirty-to-forty-year lag story. It is just not the operator's story.

## (2) Hughes and load factor — L2 reframed as demand creation, with no handoff

Yes, decisively. Insull's capacity was built *ahead* of demand as a deliberate bet on diversity, then demand was manufactured to fill it. He took the demand-meter idea from Brighton in 1894, implemented two-tier rates by 1897 (domestic bills down 32% in a year), and built Fisk Street in 1903 at 20,000 kW on the premise that off-peak recruitment — traction, ice plants, electrolytic process loads — would flatten the curve. Load factors moved from roughly 20% toward and past 50%.

This is fatal to reading L2 as accidental overbuild scavenged by outsiders. The capacity was priced into existence, and **the party who built it captured the rent from filling it**. There is no L2→L3 handoff and no change of hands. Worse for the operator: Insull's chief structural obstacle was industrial *self-generation* — Edison's own company had installed 702 isolated stations against 58 central stations by 1886 — and the canonical L3 firm, Ford, is precisely the customer Insull never won.

## (3) The utility holding-company bubble — real, missed in round 1, and it does not do the work asked of it

The bubble is well documented and round 1 should have found it. In September 1929 utilities were 18% of NYSE value ($14.8bn); utility stocks rose 48% in the first nine months of 1929 against 20% for industrials; five major operating utilities traded at 3.06–3.34× book on regulated assets that theory says should sit near book; utilities fell 55% September–November 1929, the worst of any sector; the nine largest holding companies' 1929 lows averaged 33% of their highs. Insull controlled ~$500m of assets on ~$27m of equity. Public utility investment stock growth in the mid-to-late 1920s ran near 80% of the 1929 total versus under 30% for all industries. 53 holding companies with $1.7bn of securities entered bankruptcy or receivership 1929–36; 600,000 shareholders and 500,000 bondholders were wiped out.

But the chain "crash → PUHCA/TVA/REA → universal cheap power → postwar appliance and suburb economy" fails in three places:

- **Urban electrification was already finished.** By 1930, 68% of all US homes and 84% of urban homes had service. The electrical precondition of the postwar suburb was delivered by bubble-era private utilities. What the New Deal institutions delivered was the rural residual: farms from ~10–12% in 1935 to ~80–90% by 1950. Large and real — but not the appliance economy's foundation.
- **TVA is not downstream of Insull.** Its origin is the National Defense Act of 1916 and the Muscle Shoals nitrate plant; Wilson Dam completed 1924; Norris's Muscle Shoals bill was vetoed by Hoover in 1931 as socialistic. TVA passed 18 May 1933, two years before PUHCA. The Insull collapse discredited the private-power lobby and lowered the political price — a real second-order channel, not the cause.
- **No distressed-asset transfer occurred.** Generating capacity grew ~100% in the 1920s and only ~25% in the 1930s; federal hydro was 20% of *new* capacity 1931–41. The New Deal built new plant; it did not buy wreckage at cents on the dollar. PUHCA dismantled the pyramids *above* the operating companies. Commonwealth Edison survived Insull. The operating utilities of 1926 are largely those of 1956. **The "different people" prediction fails outright.**

There is also a framework cost: the operator now has two rival L2 candidates inside one L1 story — shop-floor reorganisation (1900–1930) and the utility bubble (1922–1932) — with different agents, dates and successors. That deepens round 1's non-uniqueness problem rather than resolving it.

## (4) The WWII tail — cut it

**Financing.** The DPC alone put ~$9.2bn into 2,300+ facilities, roughly two-thirds of all new private industrial capacity added over the period; about two-thirds of ~$25bn total wartime industrial facility value was direct federal money. Half of DPC funds went to aircraft; the largest single item was $176m for Dodge's Chicago aircraft-engine plant.

**Ford's wartime capacity was new, not converted.** The Rouge aircraft-engine facility was a new $23m building (contract October 1940). Willow Run was an entirely new plant begun March 1941, $47.6m for building and equipment, designated Air Force Plant 31, government-owned and Ford-operated; Ford initially refused DPC financing and built-then-sold, transferring the land to the RFC's DPC in July 1944, and declined its postwar repurchase option (Kaiser-Frazer bought it, then GM in 1953).

**The share question cannot be answered from public sources.** The govinfo tabulation *War Industrial Facilities Authorized July 1940–August 1945* lists authorisations by corporation and by public versus private funds but does not split new construction from expansion/conversion in the portion I could retrieve. **I will not estimate it.** What is firm: Donald Nelson's industry-of-origin figures (auto makers >20% of total US war output, >50% of aircraft engines, 33% of machine guns, 80% of tanks and tank parts, 100% of trucks) are routinely misread as evidence for *converted commercial plant*. They are not; much of that output came from federally financed new plant operated by auto firms. That conflation is precisely Wilson's target.

**Did the technique transfer?** Partially, painfully, with a two-and-a-half-year lag, and it was substantially rebuilt en route. Ford imported its tooling philosophy — hard steel dies where the aircraft industry used soft tooling — needing 30,000+ dies for 1,225,000 parts, equivalent to eight or nine car model changeovers. That gave the eventual volume and also caused the failure: hard dies froze the design against constant Army modification. A 1943 Congressional committee found Ford had built a line that too closely resembled an automobile assembly line, "despite the warning of many experienced aircraft[men]." Labour churn destroyed the other precondition (January 1943: 2,900 hired, 3,100 lost). Sorensen — who had installed Ford's first conveyor in 1912 — was displaced by Mead Bricker in autumn 1943. Resolution came from outsourcing to ~1,000 suppliers plus a design freeze, not purer Fordism. **But "Willow Run failed" is too strong**: peak 428 Liberators in August 1944; 6,791 assembled plus 1,893 knock-down kits, ~8,684 of roughly 18,500 B-24s. Ford's Rouge engine learning curve was real: 2,331 hours per engine falling to 1,028 by end-1944. Note also Ford was not the auto industry's leading war producer — Chrysler >20,000 tanks and tank destroyers, GM Fisher Body >16,000, Ford 1,683 M-4s and 1,035 M-10s; Ford made 14.5% of US military vehicles.

**The macro finding that ends the argument.** Field: manufacturing TFP fell −1.4%/yr 1941–48, −3.7%/yr 1941–44, −5.1%/yr 1941–45; learning was product-specific and largely worthless once the wartime output mix ended. Separately, Field puts peak twentieth-century TFP growth in the 1929–41 window. Gordon disagrees (~3.5%/yr in the 1940s, credited partly to the war). The dispute is live, so the WWII tail cannot be cited as settled — and on the Field side it is negative.
stress.implications_for_framework: **Breaks the example as stated; qualifies the framework hard; and puts the "different people" clause in serious trouble.** Example (a) cannot be published in the form "electricity → shop-floor reorganisation → assembly line, cheap cars, WWII mobilisation." Cut the WWII tail entirely — it is federally financed new capacity with contested-to-negative measured productivity effects, captured by the state and by firms that mostly did not keep the assets. Reclassify the assembly line from "L3 of electrification" to a converging, independently-originated trajectory that became complementary to L2 and accelerated it — which is how David and Wright, the framework's own authorities, classify it. That is a topological change, not a detail: it means the real structure is a lattice of converging trajectories rather than a chain of derivatives, which makes round 1's non-uniqueness problem strictly worse, because in a lattice "which layer is this" has no answer even in principle. The "different people" clause fails at every surviving joint of this case: Ford electrified Ford's own plant and Ford built Ford's line; Insull built the capacity and Insull engineered the demand that filled it; Commonwealth Edison outlived the collapse of its own parent and kept its customers. What survives — and is worth keeping, because it is clean and quantified — is a narrower example: L1 = practical electric power (1880s–1900s); L2 = a twenty-year no-payoff installation period of group-drive retrofit (1899–1919) plus a genuine financial frenzy in utility holding companies (~1922–1932) that funded supply-side scale and interconnection; L3 = the 1919–29 manufacturing reorganisation on unit drive and single-storey linear layout, delivering industrial TFP of ~5–6%/yr against ~1%/yr before. Lag L1 to payoff: thirty to forty years. Also add the utility bubble to the case file as the framework's best-documented *counter*-case on value capture: a large, textbook Perez frenzy whose physical legacy was redistributed through the same incumbents under new regulation, with no third generation and no change of hands. If the framework is to remain falsifiable, it must now specify ex ante which of two simultaneous candidate L2s (organisational versus financial) governs a given L1, and it must state what evidence would count as the "different people" clause failing — because on the flagship case it already has.

testable_propositions: Within-firm sequencing test: for any L1 general-purpose technology, the firm that builds the canonical L3 business will be in the top quintile of adopters of the SHALLOW form of L2 and in the middle or bottom of the distribution on the DEEP form. Ford: 100% electric group drive in 1910 when the national aggregate was ~30%; still line-shaft-constrained in 1919; single-storey plants only from 1922. If this pattern does not replicate on internet-to-cloud (e.g. Amazon's dark-fibre and datacentre adoption relative to peers), the frontier-versus-average defence of the ordering problem collapses.

Value-capture test on utilities: if the framework's 'different people' clause is right, the operating companies that survived the 1932 holding-company collapse should have lost share to post-crash entrants over 1935-1955. Prediction from this research: they did not. Commonwealth Edison and its peers retained their franchises and customers; the losers were top-tier holding-company securityholders. Any case where the frenzy's physical assets are redistributed through the SAME incumbents under new regulation is a framework counter-case, and utilities is the largest one available.

Distressed-asset-transfer test: a genuine L2 bubble should produce a measurable transfer of physical assets at a large discount to book to parties who did not build them. Telecom 2001-04 passes (Cogent: ~$14bn book for ~$60m). US electric utilities 1932-38 should fail this test on any measure of generating or transmission assets changing hands below book to new entrants. If it fails, 'financial bubble' and 'productive overbuild' are separable and the framework must say which one it requires.

Demand-creation versus overbuild test: where an L2 builder can price-discriminate across time-of-use, capacity built ahead of demand will be filled by the builder and no L3 handoff will occur. Insull is the type case. Prediction: L3 handoffs occur only where the L2 builder cannot capture the complementary demand — i.e. where the asset is non-excludable, stranded by bankruptcy, or subject to a regulated rate of return that caps the builder's upside.

Productivity-window test: for electrification the measurable payoff window is 1919-29 (industrial TFP ~5-6%/yr against ~1%/yr for 1899-1914), not 1941-45 (manufacturing TFP -5.1%/yr per Field). The framework should predict, for any L1, that the payoff window coincides with the switch to the DEEP form of L2 and terminates before any war mobilisation. Any framework version that claims a war-mobilisation tail as L3 payoff must first defeat Field.

Layer-uniqueness test (the round-1 problem, sharpened): where a single L1 admits two simultaneous candidate L2s with different agents — an organisational one (group-to-unit drive, 1899-1929) and a financial one (utility holding companies, 1922-32) — the framework must nominate one ex ante on a stated criterion and be wrong if the other turns out to carry the causal weight. Electricity is the test case, and as it stands the framework cannot make the nomination.

Transfer-of-technique test: mass-production technique transplanted from a high-volume, design-stable product to a low-volume, design-unstable one will fail on first attempt and require a design freeze plus supplier disaggregation before it works. Willow Run: hard steel dies, 30,000+ dies for 1,225,000 parts, a critical 1943 Congressional finding, Sorensen displaced autumn 1943, resolution via ~1,000 suppliers and a frozen design, peak 428 aircraft/month only in August 1944. The framework should predict this lag structure wherever an L3 technique is exported across a product-volatility gradient.

stress.headline_finding: The attack premise handed to me is factually false as stated, and its failure rescues the operator on the narrow point while exposing a worse problem elsewhere. US CS bachelor's degree production did not collapse "40-50% between 2000 and 2007." It ROSE 57% from 1999-2000 (37,788) to its all-time peak in 2003-04 (59,488), then fell 36% to a trough of 37,992 in 2008-09 — a level still slightly ABOVE the bubble-peak year (NCES Digest tables dt12_349, dt20_325.35). Master's production never once fell below its 1999-2000 level (14,990) and was 19% above it by 2008-09 (17,907); doctorates more than doubled, 779 (1999-2000) to 1,698 (2007-08). The graduate pipeline that produces distributed-systems people expanded monotonically through the entire bust. What collapsed was ENROLMENT INTENT, which is a leading indicator with a four-year lag: newly declared majors at Taulbee departments fell from 15,958 (fall 2000) to 7,952 (fall 2005), and HERI/CIRP freshman CS intentions fell ~70% fall 2000 to 2005 (CRA CRN, March 2006). So the frenzy-enrolled cohort graduated INTO the bust, in record numbers, in 2002-2005. But the thing that actually breaks under forensic pressure is not the skills channel — it is the operator's "usually DIFFERENT PEOPLE" clause. Three of the four named L3 exemplars (AWS, Netflix, Google) are bubble-era firms run by bubble-era people who simply did not die. That is the same error class as the round-1 Cogent/Internap correction, and it is a survivorship error, not a skills error.
stress.analysis:
## (1) Degrees: the attack premise is wrong, and the corrected data supports the operator

NCES/IPEDS, CS and information sciences, bachelor's conferred: 1994-95 24,737; 1998-99 30,552; 1999-2000 37,788; 2000-01 44,142; 2001-02 50,365; 2002-03 57,433; **2003-04 59,488 (peak)**; 2004-05 54,111; 2005-06 47,702; 2006-07 42,164; 2007-08 38,523; **2008-09 37,992 (trough)**; 2009-10 39,593; 2010-11 43,066; then 59,586 (2014-15) and 88,633 (2018-19).

Peak-to-trough is -36.1% over 2004→2009, not -40-50% over 2000→2007. Over the window the attack actually named (1999-2000 to 2006-07), production *rose* 11.6%.

Master's: 14,990 (1999-2000) → 20,143 (2003-04) → trough 16,232 (2006-07) → 17,907 (2008-09). Doctorates: 779 → 1,698 (2007-08), a 118% increase straight through the crash. **The bust did not destroy the training pipeline for the people who build cloud infrastructure. It expanded it.**

Enrolment is the separate, genuinely collapsing series, and the lag explains everything: CRA reports Taulbee-department bachelor's fell 17% in one year (AY2003/04→2004/05, to 11,808), and new majors halved 2000→2005. The frenzy recruited the largest CS cohort in history in 1998-2000; the crash dumped it onto the market in 2002-2005 at depressed wages. That is a *stronger* version of the operator's claim than the operator makes.

## (2) Employment: sectorally asymmetric, and the asymmetry matters

Telecom carriers: +300,000 jobs 1996 to early 2001; then -17%, over 200,000 jobs, 2001-2003, returning to roughly 1997 levels (Rutgers Heldrich, *Changing Structure of the Telecommunications Industry*). BLS reports wired-telecom hours declining almost every year since the 2000 peak. That employment never came back.

Software/IT services: the dip bottomed in 2002; IT unemployment peaked 2003 and normalised by 2005; **US IT employment exceeded its bubble peak from 2005 onward** (Panko, *IT employment prospects: beyond the dotcom bubble*, EJIS 17(3), 2008). Computer systems design and related services added 232,300 jobs, +18%, 2001-2011 (BLS).

This decomposition is fatal to a simple "the bubble left skills" story. The layer that was physically overbuilt (carriers) had its workforce destroyed permanently. The layer that produced L3 (software, distributed systems, web operations) barely contracted and recovered inside four years. **The fibre and the skills were left behind by different halves of the bubble, and only one of those halves is traceable into L3.**

I could not retrieve BLS CES series CES5051700001 (telecom) or CES6054150001 (computer systems design) year-by-year: fred.stlouisfed.org, bls.gov PDFs and stlouisfed.org all returned 403 to the fetch tool, and the sandbox blocked curl. **Pull those two series directly before publishing.** Everything in this paragraph is secondary-sourced.

## (3) Where the engineers went — confirmed, and a large hole

Confirmed person-level transfers:
- **Mick Mountz**: ~6 months at Webvan (2000), observed ~70% of fulfilment-centre cost was human picking; founded **Kiva Systems** (2003) with Peter Wurman and Raffaello D'Andrea; Amazon acquired it March 2012 for ~$775m; rebranded Amazon Robotics 2015. Textbook L2 failure → L3 capability.
- **Chris Pinkham**: founded TICSA, South Africa's first ISP (1993), sold to UUNET 1996; joined Amazon 2000 to run network engineering; hired Benjamin Black 2002; the two wrote the 2003 vision paper for standardised, automated, web-service infrastructure; Bezos approved 2004; Pinkham built EC2 in Cape Town with Christopher Brown and Willem van Biljon; launched 2006. **ISP-era operator → AWS.**
- **Milo Medin**: co-founder/CTO @Home Network (f. 11 July 1996; peak 4.1m subscribers, $35bn market cap, ~1,350 staff; Chapter 11 on 1 Oct 2001; all staff laid off by Q1 2002; network sold to AT&T for $307m) → M2Z Networks (2005) → Google VP Access Services (2010), ran Google Fiber.
- **Naval Ravikant**: @Home (1996) → Epinions → AngelList. **Joe Kraus**: Excite → JotSpot → acquired by Google 2006 → GV.
- **Jeff Dean** (DEC Western Research Lab, Palo Alto, 1996-99), **Sanjay Ghemawat** (DEC Systems Research Center, 130 Lytton Ave, Palo Alto), **Luiz Barroso** (DEC WRL) → all to Google in 1999. They built MapReduce, GFS, BigTable and warehouse-scale computing — the literal technical core of the L3 cloud layer.

Note the dates, because they wound the thesis. Dean/Ghemawat/Barroso moved in **1999**, during the frenzy, triggered by Compaq's 1998 acquisition of DEC — not by the dot-com crash. Pinkham joined Amazon in 2000. Medin's Google move was 2010, nine years after @Home died, via an intervening venture. **The best-documented human-capital transfers into L3 were not caused by the bust.**

**The hole**: I found no systematic public evidence — no matched employer-employee study, no inventor-mobility study, no founder-history dataset — tracing where WorldCom's, Global Crossing's or 360networks' engineers went. The BLS Displaced Workers Survey records 5.3m workers displaced from 3+ year jobs Jan 2001-Dec 2003, with mean earnings decline jumping from 0.9% (1997-99) to 13.7% (2001-03), but I found no published dot-com/telecom disaggregation. **The telecom-engineer destination question is unanswered in public data. Any claim about it would be anecdote.**

## (4) The one systematic law behind the channel — and it is not about bubbles

Babina, *Destructive Creation at Work: How Financial Distress Spurs Entrepreneurship*, RFS 33(9):4061-4101 (2020), US Census matched employer-employee data. Firm financial distress accelerates employee exit to entrepreneurship; the effect is amplified in high-tech and services; distress-driven founders earned higher wages pre-exit and their startups showed higher employment and payroll growth than typical startups; and the effect is **mitigated where non-compete contracts are enforceable**. (I could not retrieve point estimates — paywalled at OUP; directions and qualitative magnitudes only, from the Census working paper 17-19 abstract.)

Read that carefully. The mechanism is **firm distress**, not bubble. Any distress does it. A bubble is simply a distress-generating machine operating at scale and in synchrony. DEC/Compaq was not a bubble event and it produced Google's entire infrastructure brain trust.

## (5) Saxenian, and two corrections to the operator's framing

First correction: "Route 128's collapse produced nothing" is false. Route 128's collapse produced Greater Boston biotech, now arguably the world's leading life-sciences cluster. What Boston failed to do was regenerate *within computing*. The region recovered; the sectoral human capital did not recycle in-sector.

Second, and sharper: DEC's most valuable computing human capital **did** recycle — but it was DEC's *California* operations. SRC (Palo Alto, founded 1984 by Bob Taylor and colleagues out of Xerox PARC) and WRL (Palo Alto, 1982). Dean, Ghemawat and Barroso went from those Palo Alto labs into Google. Massachusetts DEC produced no comparable computing lineage. (A9.com, Amazon's research arm, later occupied the Lytton Avenue building.) **Same firm, same failure, two labour markets, opposite outcomes.** That is close to a natural experiment and it points at institutions, not at the bubble.

The institutional evidence stack:
- **Gilson**, NYU L. Rev. 74:575-629 (1999): Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600 voids non-competes — an accident of 1870s codification. Supplies the legal mechanism for Saxenian's cultural observation.
- **Fallick, Fleischman & Rebitzer**, REStat 88(3):472-481 (2006): college-educated men in Silicon Valley's computer industry job-hop more than in out-of-state computer clusters — *and other California computer clusters match Silicon Valley's rate*. That comparison implicates state law rather than Valley culture. Cleanest identification available.
- **Marx, Strumsky & Fleming**, Mgmt Sci 55(6):875-889 (2009): Michigan's inadvertent 1985 non-compete reversal, diff-in-diff; enforcement attenuates inventor mobility, most for firm-specific and narrow-specialty inventors.

Conclusion: the crash is the shock; non-enforceability is the transmission mechanism. **The L2→L3 skills channel is conditional on labour-market institutions, not automatic.**

## (6) The quantity argument that kills the attack outright

Even granting a 36% degree collapse, did it bind? Google: 3,021 employees (2004) → 5,680 (2005) → 10,700 (2006) → 16,800 (2007) → 20,200 (2008) → 24,400 (2010). That is roughly 21,400 net hires, globally, all functions, over six years. Facebook had a few hundred people in 2007. Against a US CS bachelor's flow that never fell below 37,992/year, master's above 16,000/year, and a total US IT workforce in the millions. **The L3 firms of 2005-2010 were microscopic relative to labour supply.** The pipeline contraction could not possibly have constrained them; it only began to bite around 2012-2015, by which point degree production had already recovered past its 2004 peak.

## (7) The immigration gap the operator has no account of

US computer-science workforce roughly doubled, 0.82m (1995) → 1.53m (2001), with the immigrant share rising from 14% to 25.7% (Richmond Fed). The H-1B cap ran 65,000 → 115,000 (1999) → 195,000 (2001) → **back to 65,000 from FY2004**. So a quarter of the bubble-era skill stock was foreign-born, and the visa channel was throttled exactly as L3 began scaling; India took roughly 60% of the global offshoring market in the 2000s. A meaningful fraction of the "skills residue" left the country or was never in it. The operator's framework currently has no term for this.

## (8) What actually breaks: the "different people" clause

- **AWS**: built inside Amazon (f.1994, IPO 1997 — a bubble-era firm), by Amazon's own network-engineering leadership, approved by Bezos. Same firm, same era, same people.
- **Netflix**: Reed Hastings, founded 1997. Bubble-era founder, same person, pivoted to streaming in 2007.
- **Google**: founded 1998; Page, Brin, Hölzle, Dean, Ghemawat all in place by 1999.
- Only **Cloudflare** (2009) and **Facebook** (2004) are clean generational breaks.

Three of four named L3 exemplars are bubble-era firms whose founders survived the crash and bought the wreckage. This is the Cogent/Internap error again: **mistaking survivors for successors.** In the skills domain the generational-turnover claim is weakest of all, because the skills frequently did not need to move firms — the firms merely had to not die.
stress.implications_for_framework: QUALIFIES sharply, and BREAKS one named sub-claim. The skills half of example (b) survives, but only after two amendments that cost the operator real ground. First, the mechanism must be restated. The bubble did not TRAIN a generation — the university and immigration systems did that, and the university pipeline shrank 36% while the visa channel was cut from 195,000 to 65,000. What L2 supplied was LIQUIDATION: it dissolved the firm-specific bonds holding experienced operators in place and made their time cheap. Recommended publishable formulation: "L2's durable contribution to labour is not training but liquidation. Whether released operators become L3 capability depends on whether the local labour market permits recombination — a legal and institutional variable (non-compete enforceability, at-will norms, dense local VC), not a property of the bubble." That restatement has the additional virtue of being falsifiable, which is exactly what the round-1 reference-frame problem demands: it predicts that identical shocks in enforcing versus non-enforcing jurisdictions produce different L3 formation rates, and Babina (2020), Marx et al. (2009) and Fallick et al. (2006) already partly test it. Second, the telecom half of the skills claim is UNSUPPORTED and must be dropped or explicitly flagged as unevidenced. There is no public tracing of WorldCom, Global Crossing or 360networks engineers, and carrier employment never recovered. The operator may keep the fibre claim; he may not currently keep a telecom skills claim. Third and most damaging: the "usually DIFFERENT PEOPLE" clause fails on example (b)'s own exemplar list. AWS, Netflix and Google are bubble-era firms run by bubble-era people. That is a survivorship error of the same class already caught with Cogent and Internap, and it recurring twice suggests it is systematic rather than incidental. Either downgrade the clause to "different firms OR the same firms recapitalised, with the value accruing to whoever holds the cospecialised assets after the price collapse" (which is just Teece 1986 and is defensible), or restrict the strong generational claim to cases where it actually holds. Do not publish it as a general feature. Net: example (b) is still the strongest case in the set, but it is now a case about labour-market institutions and asset repricing, not about bubbles as schools.

stress.headline_finding: The ASP-to-SaaS natural experiment — which the operator correctly identified as the highest-value test — comes back NEGATIVE, and it takes half of example (b) with it. Bandwidth price cannot explain why ASPs died in 1999-2001 and SaaS worked by 2006, because bandwidth was under 1% of ASP revenue even at peak-1998 transit prices; a cost line that small cannot bind, and a 100x fall in it changes nothing. The contemporaneous post-mortem (Computerworld, 29 Oct 2001) explicitly lists cheap bandwidth as an *enabler* of the ASP market, not a missing input, and attributes failure to single-tenant architecture, lift-and-shift of client/server apps, customization demands, manual provisioning and datacenter capex. The controlled comparison is decisive: Salesforce was founded in March 1999 — inside the frenzy, on identical input prices to Corio and USinternetworking — and survived on multi-tenancy. Same infrastructure, opposite outcomes. Worse for the operator's list, AWS's documented founding rationale (Benjamin Black's own account of the 2003 Black/Pinkham proposal to Bezos) contains no bandwidth, network-capacity or fibre-pricing reasoning whatsoever — it was about standardization, uniformity, automated provisioning and web-service APIs — and Werner Vogels has separately said the excess-capacity origin story is a myth. AWS and Azure do not belong in a fibre-bubble causal chain. Separately, and independently, the demand-side challenge lands: for streaming video the binding constraint was last-mile, not backbone. Two partial rescues: no new US national long-haul network was built from the late 1990s until roughly 2015-17, which is the single strongest fact in the operator's favour; and the last mile had its own bubble and its own residue (@Home's Chapter 11, the DSL CLEC wipeout, the AT&T Broadband unwind), which lets the operator keep the *shape* of the story if he changes its referent.
stress.analysis:
## (1) The central unknown datum: not public, and the number everyone quotes is a misquote

There is no authoritative public dataset for what fraction of US fibre laid 1996-2001 had been lit by 2010, by whom, or at what price. State this plainly rather than estimating. The FCC never collected strand-level lit/dark inventories (Form 477 measures broadband subscription, not strand-miles); the only strand inventories are commercial products from TeleGeography, CRU/KMI and CIR, none published at "% lit by year" granularity; and IRU prices are contractually private.

The figure that circulates — "only 2.7% of the fibre was ever lit" — is a corruption of a single-city datapoint. Its provenance is a Network World article of 8 September 2003 citing TeleGeography's Alan Mauldin on 2002 data: of long-haul fibre passing through **Chicago**, 3.9% was lit, and of that **lit** capacity, 2.7% was dedicated to IP. The 2.7% is IP's share of lit capacity in one city, not the national lit fraction. If the operator has used the 2.7% figure, it must come out.

The same article carries a fact that cuts against the naive glut story: a TeleChoice study (July 2001) examining 22 intercity US routes found already-lit capacity at 70%+ utilisation on 14 of them. The correct picture is a vast surplus of *dark strands and conduit* alongside reasonably utilised *operating transmission systems*. Lighting a strand requires DWDM terminals, amplifiers, regen huts and power; the WDM equipment market collapsed from $5.1bn (2000) to $376m (2002) to an estimated $269m (2003) per RHK's Ron Kline. So the residue's value did not come from strands being lit later. It came from (a) DWDM channel density rising by orders of magnitude on the *same* strands and (b) the write-down of the capital base, which reset the price of transport for a decade and a half.

On the cost-base question: **AWS ≈ zero, Netflix ≈ zero, Google unknown-but-nonzero.** Amazon's cost base is servers, memory, disks, power and datacenter shells; it has never disclosed a network line item, and its founding rationale was not an input-price story. Netflix bought no fibre in the relevant period — it rented CDN, paying roughly $0.03/GB across Limelight and Level 3 in March 2009 (Rayburn), about $0.015/GB from Akamai for a couple of months in early 2010 before reverting to ~$0.06/GB, and signing Level 3 as primary CDN in November 2010. Its total online-video spend was ~$40m in 2007 rising toward ~$100m in 2009 against revenue in the $1.2-1.7bn range. Google did buy dark fibre — it began issuing DWDM RFPs in early 2005 — but has never disclosed volumes or prices. Not public.

This exposes a mis-specification in the framework's value-capture step. **The L3 winners did not buy the L2 assets. They bought services priced off the L2 assets' written-down replacement cost.** The firms that actually bought the assets — Cogent (~$14bn book from 13 carriers for ~$60m, 2001-04), Level 3 (WilTel for $680m: 115m shares plus ~$386m cash, closed 23 December 2005), Zayo — earn utility returns. That is a price mechanism, not an asset-transfer mechanism, and it is a better and more defensible claim than the one the operator is currently making.

## (2) Demand side: the last mile wins, and the framework is missing a layer

For streaming video the binding constraint was access, not backbone.

Pew home-broadband adoption among US adults: 3% (2000), 6% (2001), 11% (2002), 16% (2003), 24% (2004), 33% (2005), 42% (2006), 47% (2007), 66% (2010). Netflix launched Watch Now on 16 January 2007 with 1,000 titles at 47% penetration; streams overtook DVD shipments only around 2009-11 as penetration crossed 60%. Akamai puts the US average connection at 3.8 Mbps in Q4 2009 rising to 4.6 Mbps in Q2 2010, against a Netflix top HD stream needing ~4.8 Mbps: **the average American connection could not sustain Netflix HD until roughly 2011.** Meanwhile the backbone was in surplus from 2001 onward and never binding again.

Contemporaries said the same thing. TeleGeography found the six most competitive US metros had total intracity bandwidth 50% *below* the long-haul bandwidth transiting them, and only ~10% of US business locations had fibre to them. The 2003 Network World framing is that abundant long-haul was unreachable because of the access bottleneck.

The capital that fixed the access network was largely not bubble residue: cable invested ~$65bn 1996-2002, ~$100bn cumulatively by end-2005 and ~$213bn since 1996 (NCTA); DOCSIS 1.0 (March 1997), 1.1 (April 1999), 2.0 (December 2001), 3.0 (August 2006, mass deployment 2008-11); Verizon spent ~$23bn on FiOS 2004-2010 before halting expansion. Incumbent operating cash flow, not distressed assets.

**But the last mile had its own bubble.** Excite@Home — 4 million residential broadband subscribers — filed Chapter 11 in September 2001; AT&T agreed to buy its broadband access assets for $307m; Comcast and Cox each paid $160m for continuity of service. The DSL CLECs (NorthPoint, Rhythms, Covad) were destroyed in 2000-01. AT&T's cable adventure (TCI 1998, MediaOne 2000) destroyed tens of billions before the assets landed with Comcast in 2002; Adelphia went bankrupt the same year. So the HFC plant that carried Netflix was substantially built during the same 1996-2002 capital-markets episode and its equity was substantially destroyed. The operator can keep the structure by relocating the referent from long-haul strands to access-network overbuild. He cannot keep it as written.

There is also a layer the framework has no slot for at all: **the codec and device stack.** H.264 standardised 2003; Flash Player 9 Update 3 added H.264 on 3 December 2007; Netflix moved to Silverlight in 2008; Roku shipped May 2008; Xbox 360 got Netflix on 19 November 2008 and was the first device to carry it in HD. Netflix streaming was browser-only for its first eighteen months and did not reach the television — where the demand was — until late 2008. No quantity of fibre or DOCSIS produces Netflix without H.264 and a $99 box. This layer is pure Bresnahan-Trajtenberg co-invention: no bubble, no overbuild, no malinvestment, no restructuring. A necessary capital-intensive non-bubble layer sitting between L2 and L3 is a structural gap in the theory, not a detail.

## (3) The ASP experiment: negative, and it is the cleanest result here

The arithmetic. Take 1998 transit at the commonly cited ~$1,200/Mbps/month (I could not verify the DrPeering year-by-year table this session — three 403s — but the qualitative finding of ~61% average annual decline 1998-2010 is attributed to Norton). One Mbps sustained for a month moves ~328 GB, so ~$3.66/GB. A browser CRM or expense-report session moves single-digit MB per user per day; at 5 MB/day, ~150 MB/month, that is ~$0.55/user/month against ASP price points of $50-200. **Under 1% of revenue at the worst prices in the sample.** The result is robust to the transit figure being wrong by 3x in either direction.

The fairest counter is that many ASPs delivered thick client/server apps over Citrix or Terminal Services at ~30 kbps sustained, which is ~2.2 GB/user/month, or ~$8/user/month at 1998 prices — 4-16% of the price point. Material, but not fatal, and note that the SaaS answer to that cost was to stop using Citrix and write for the browser. That is architecture again, not input price.

What actually changed: multi-tenancy (reported per-customer operating cost $12,000-$18,000/year for single-tenant ASPs versus under $2,000 for multi-tenant SaaS — a ~10x unit-economics change requiring no infrastructure precondition); owning rather than hosting the application; self-service signup and per-seat card billing versus manual provisioning; XMLHttpRequest/AJAX going mainstream in 2005, which fixed *latency* perception (not a bandwidth problem, and not fixed by cheap fibre); and commodity LAMP/x86 collapsing the serving tier. Salesforce, founded March 1999, is the control: same cohort, same input prices, different architecture, opposite outcome.

**The fibre story does not carry the SaaS/cloud leg. It carries the video leg only, where bandwidth is a first-order cost.**

## (4) Ex-ante forecasts exist, and the interesting finding is not the one expected

The three verifiers who asserted nobody ever forecasts an L3 in advance were wrong, and none of them looked.

Gilder's *Telecosm* (2000) forecast that the bottleneck would move from processing to communications, that bandwidth would become abundant, and that the winning strategy was to waste it — his phrasing about learning "how to waste bandwidth" (attributed) is the AWS/YouTube/Netflix business model stated five to eight years early. Right in kind. He was also catastrophically wrong on firms, promoting telecom equities at the peak through the Gilder Technology Report, and wrong on television. **That is the operator's "different people" claim confirmed from the other side: correct forecast, destroyed forecaster.**

More damaging to the "nobody saw it" line: utility computing was forecast, funded and executed by incumbents *before* AWS, and they lost anyway. HP created a Utility Computing Division in 1998 explicitly to build a "computing power plant" and launched the Utility Data Center in 2001. Sun announced a cloud concept in 2000 and launched Sun Grid in March 2006 at $1/CPU-hour — the same month S3 shipped, five months before EC2, at roughly 10x EC2's small-instance price; Oracle killed it on 7 March 2010. Alexa launched a paid utility-computing search platform in December 2005. Reed Hastings named the company Netflix in 1997 rather than DVDs-by-mail on an explicit expectation of internet delivery.

And the counter-example that should be foregrounded: AWS itself was *not* built on a bandwidth thesis and did not consume residue.

## Unverified, flagged

DrPeering's year-by-year transit table (403 on all attempts); Salesforce revenue figures; Global Crossing's reported $250m-for-61% sale to ST Telemedia; Level 3's reported ~$242m for Genuity; the dating of Gilder's "Fibersphere" essays. Web search budget was exhausted before these could be closed.
stress.implications_for_framework: QUALIFIES SEVERELY, AND BREAKS ONE HALF. Example (b) as written — "internet → dot-com and fibre/telecom bubbles → AWS, Azure, Cloudflare, Netflix" — must be split into two examples, because it currently fuses a chain where the mechanism holds with a chain where a natural experiment falsifies it. (i) The VIDEO/CDN chain survives and is quantifiable: transport fell from ~$3.66/GB implied at 1998 transit to ~$0.03/GB CDN in 2009, taking the delivery cost of a two-hour film from a few dollars to about five cents, and no new US national long-haul network was built from the late 1990s to roughly 2015-17. That last fact should replace the "% dark fibre" statistic as the headline evidence; the 2.7% figure is a misquoted single-city datapoint and must be struck. (ii) The CLOUD/SaaS chain does not survive. The ASP-to-SaaS experiment isolates architecture (multi-tenancy) as the causal variable on constant input prices, with Salesforce as a same-cohort control; and AWS's documented 2003 origin contains no bandwidth reasoning at all. AWS and Azure should be removed from example (b); Cloudflare (f. 2009) is the only well-chosen name on the list. Three further corrections. First, the value-capture step is mis-specified: L3 firms bought SERVICES priced off written-down assets, not the assets themselves; the actual asset buyers (Cogent, Level 3, Zayo) earn utility returns. Restate the mechanism as input-price reset, not asset transfer — it is stronger and it is what the evidence supports. Second, the physical residue that mattered for consumer video was the ACCESS-network overbuild (HFC 1996-2002, the DSL CLEC wipeout, @Home's Chapter 11 with 4m subscribers, the AT&T Broadband unwind), not long-haul strands; the framework currently omits it entirely while claiming the long-haul story. Third, and most structurally: the framework has no slot for a necessary, capital-intensive, NON-bubble layer between L2 and L3 — DOCSIS 3.0 and FiOS's ~$23bn funded from incumbent cash flow, plus H.264, Flash's December 2007 H.264 build, Silverlight, Roku and the Xbox. Streaming is impossible without it and none of it is malinvestment residue. If the theory cannot accommodate a mandatory non-bubble intermediate layer, it is not a theory of how value arrives; it is a theory about one contributing input. On the Round-1 unfalsifiability problem: the "nobody forecasts L3" defence collapses — Gilder, HP's 1998 Utility Computing Division, Sun Grid at $1/CPU-hour in March 2006, and Hastings naming Netflix in 1997 are all ex-ante and right in kind. That is net GOOD for the framework, because the forecasts were right in kind while the forecasters and the incumbents who acted on them were destroyed, which is the "different people" claim independently confirmed. But it does nothing for the layer-indexing problem, which remains the programme's binding weakness.

cases.transmission_mechanism: L2 malinvestment proposed but never completed. No L3 company harvested stranded assets. Unlike Iridium (physical satellites operational, low-cost restart possible) or Globalstar (constellation complete, transferable), Teledesic's project remained incomplete—no asset to transfer, no L3 to capture. Framework predicts L2 overcapacity enables L3; Teledesic is null case (L2 aborted before completion).
cases.who_captured_value: No L3 identified; project terminated; capital destroyed
cases.lag_years: Founding 1994; peak spending ~1998-2000; suspension Oct 1 2002 = project abandoned before L3-enabling asset completion
sources: https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20021007/teledesic070/the-birth-and-demise-of-an-idea-teledesics-internet-in-the-sky
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teledesic

cases.name: Merchant Power CCGT Overbuild and Fragmented Asset Sales
cases.primary: Combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power generation technology
cases.secondary: 1992-2002 merchant power overbuild: 21.9 GW capacity added (~$250B invested), bankruptcies Calpine (2005 Chapter 11, $26.6B assets/$22.5B debt), Mirant (2003), NRG (2003), PG&E; total value destroyed $150-200B (2002-2006 write-offs)
third_order: NRG Energy acquired Dynegy's 1,800 MW California capacity; later acquired Texas Genco (2006)
Aquila purchased Aries power plant from Calpine ($158.5M, 580 MW)
Calpine sold Lockport minority stake (11.4%, 200 MW) to Fortistar (~$27M, 2002)
Calpine sold De Pere plant to Wisconsin Public Service ($120M, 180 MW)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Plants sold from bankrupt L2 operators (Calpine, Mirant) to multiple acquirers at distressed prices 2003-2006. Transmission: physical CCGT plants remained operational but ownership transferred as original investors wrote off capital. NRG emerged strongest, acquiring 1,800 MW from Dynegy collapse. However, unlike Iridium (single L3 with unified cost model) or aircraft (consolidated into American/United/Eastern), merchant power L3 fragmented across NRG, Dynegy, Aquila, local utilities. No single L3 equivalent captured systematic value spread. ~$250B L2 investment collapsed to ~$100B residual value; L3 aquirers paid cents on dollar but fragmented acquisition prevented economic consolidation gains.
cases.who_captured_value: NRG Energy (largest single beneficiary), Aquila, Wisconsin Public Service, Fortistar, and others; fragmented, not concentrated L3 winner
cases.lag_years: Peak investment 1999-2000; bankruptcies 2003-2005; asset sales 2003-2006 = 5-6 year L2-L3 lag
cases.discount_on_transfer: Highly variable; Calpine/Mirant liabilities ~$50-60B collapsed to ~$20-30B residual value; distressed sale prices ranged from 15-50% of book value depending on plant vintage and location

cases.name: 1920s Radio Boom, Crash, and Manufacturer Consolidation (Contested)
cases.primary: Radio transmission and receiver manufacturing technology
cases.secondary: Radio receiver manufacturing boom (1920-1929): 600+ manufacturers, sales $60M (1922) → $207M (1926) → $366M (1929); RCA stock $85 (1928) → $500 (summer 1929) → $114.75 (Sept 1929) → $2.625 (May 1932, 98% collapse); equity value destruction ~$50-60B nominal
third_order: NBC network founded Nov 15 1926 (RCA 50%, GE 30%, Westinghouse 20%) - during boom, not after crash
RCA-Victor (formed 1929, phonograph+radio integration) - emerged from merger, not L3 value capture
RCA stock recovered by 1950s-1960s; bought by GE 1986; Golden Age of Radio (1930s) supported broadcaster profitability but NOT receiver manufacturers
cases.transmission_mechanism: CONTESTED/INVERTED. Framework predicts L2 overcapacity → L3 harvest. Radio boom did create excess capacity (600+ manufacturers competing down prices 1927-1929), and crash did liquidate most early makers (Atwater Kent, Grigsby-Grunow failed; Western Electric exited). However: (1) NBC founded during boom (1926), not after crash, so not L3; (2) RCA-Victor recovery (1929) was DEFENSIVE consolidation, not offensive L3 harvest; (3) RCA's recovery came from (a) network monopoly (NBC), (b) manufacturing tubes/components with patent moat, not (c) harvesting stranded receiver-manufacturing capacity. Radio manufacturing consolidation benefited oligopoly (RCA, Philco, Zenith) through survival and price discipline, not by harvesting L2 overcapacity at distressed prices (framework mechanism). Contrast: Iridium L3 bought L2 constellation at 0.4% cost; RCA-Victor did not buy competitor receiver factories at fire-sale prices—it outlasted them through scale and brand.
cases.who_captured_value: RCA-Victor (through brand + tube monopoly + NBC network), Philco (brand + survival), Zenith (brand + survival); value accrued from consolidation/oligopoly discipline, not L2 harvesting
cases.lag_years: Boom peak 1929, crash Oct 1929, NBC pre-existing 1926 (inverted timing), RCA-Victor recovery 1930s-1950s = slow defensive consolidation, not fast L3 harvest
cases.discount_on_transfer: N/A - no systematic distressed-price acquisition of L2 receiver factories documented; L3 emerged through survival/elimination, not purchase
sources: https://thebubbleblog.substack.com/p/rcas-radiant-rise-and-radio-ruin
https://macovei.substack.com/p/the-birth-of-a-broadcasting-giant
https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/national-broadcasting-company-inc

cases.name: Post-WWI Aircraft Surplus → Barnstorming → Airmail Contracts → Major Carriers
cases.primary: Military aircraft production (WWI)
cases.secondary: Aircraft surplus and barnstorming era (L2): 6,000+ Jennys produced; post-1918 surplus sale $50-100 per aircraft; Curtiss acquired $20M worth (Jennys+engines) for 13 cents on dollar; thousands of surplus pilots; barnstorming 1920-1925 popularized aviation, created trained pilot base and aircraft-operations culture
third_order: Kelly Act (Contract Air Mail Act) Feb 2 1925 authorized private airmail contracts

First 5 CAM routes Nov 7 1925: (1) Colonial Air Transport CAM-1 (Boston-New York) → Eastern Airlines, (2) Robertson Aircraft CAM-2 (Chicago-St. Louis, Lindbergh) → American Airways (1930, consolidated 80+ carriers) → American Airlines, (3) National Air Transport CAM-3 (Chicago-Dallas) → United Airlines (via consolidation 1930s), (4) Western Air Express CAM-4 (Salt Lake City-Los Angeles), (5) Walter T. Varney CAM-5 (Elko-Pasco)
Airmail revenue: 95% of early airline revenues; carriers received 80% of mail revenue (~$0.80/pound rate)
By 1927: 2.5M miles flown, 22M letters delivered
By 1934: American Airlines assembled 80+ airmail carriers into single entity through acquisitions
cases.transmission_mechanism: L1 (military aircraft)→L2 (surplus+barnstorming): 6,000 Jennys sold post-WWI at 13 cents on dollar; thousands of pilots; barnstorming normalized aviation 1920-1925. L2→L3 (airmail contracts): Kelly Act (1925) enabled Post Office to contract private carriers. Airmail contracts provided 95% of early revenues, enabling Robertson/Colonial/NAT/etc. to build infrastructure, routes, and brand. These airmail operators then consolidated (Robertson+others→American Airways 1930, listed as American Airlines 1934 with 80+ merged carriers; NAT→United; Colonial→Eastern via Pitcairn Aviation). Transmission: surplus military aircraft (effectively free/cheap) + trained pilots enabled low-cost L2 barnstorming. Government mail subsidy (80% revenue) then enabled L3 carriers to build passenger networks from airmail base. By 1934, barnstorming-era knowledge and airmail-route infrastructure were embedded in American/United/Eastern as major carriers with passenger service.
cases.who_captured_value: Robertson Aircraft shareholders → American Airways/American Airlines; National Air Transport → United; Colonial Air Transport → Eastern; government airmail subsidy transferred surplus military assets (aircraft + pilot knowledge) into commercial airline equity
cases.lag_years: WWI ends Nov 1918, surplus aircraft available 1918-1920, peak barnstorming 1920-1925, Kelly Act Feb 1925, first airmail contracts Nov 1925, consolidations 1930-1934 = 12-16 year L2-L3 lag (ecosystem consolidation, not single-asset handoff)
cases.discount_on_transfer: Jennys post-WWI: ~$50-100 vs peacetime production ~$500-1000 = ~90% discount; pilot surplus: no wage cost (market compensation fell from military to civilian rates); government airmail subsidy effectively subsidized L3 at 95% of revenue (80% of ~$0.80/pound)
sources: https://www.history.com/articles/us-aviation-airmail-passenger-flight
https://airandspace.si.edu/explore/stories/air-mail
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson_Aircraft_Corporation
https://postalmuseum.si.edu/exhibition/airmail-in-america/building-the-commercial-aviation-network

new_cases.headline_finding: Infrastructure booms with COMPLETED physical assets (Iridium $5-6B constellation, Globalstar $2.5B constellation, CCGT plants $250B) enable L3 value capture through distressed-price transfer and radical cost restructuring (2-6 year lag). But ecosystem booms with INCOMPLETE or dispersed assets (Teledesic abandoned project; merchant power fragmented across multiple acquirers; 1920s radio manufacturing) either fail to produce L3 winners or produce only oligopolistic survivors, not systematic value harvesters. The framework works for completed single-asset infrastructure where ownership transfer is feasible; it breaks when (a) L2 never completes (Teledesic), (b) L2 assets fragment across many acquirers with no consolidating L3 (merchant power, radio manufacturing), or (c) L3 emerges during L2 boom, not after L2 crash (NBC 1926, radio networks 1930s). Iridium and post-WWI aviation are the only clean confirmations; the others reveal layer-assignment is non-unique and timing is indexical to where you begin counting.

new_cases.lens: Third-derivative framework: primary innovations (L1) create value only after bubble/malinvestment phases (L2) enable third-generation businesses (L3) that capture most value, typically long lag and different people

cases.name: The 2000 Genomics Bubble
cases.primary: DNA sequencing technology: Celera's shotgun sequencing method and publicly-funded Human Genome Project established the technical capability
cases.secondary: 2000-2001 genomics bubble: Celera Genomics (founded May 1998, $300M investment) peaked at $14B market cap in early 2000, crashed to $37 by mid-2001. Incyte collapsed when government-released free genomic data destroyed the proprietary data business model (2000). Human Genome Sciences failed. Peak capex: 2000-2001.
third_order: Illumina: founded April 1998, IPO July 2000 ($100M), acquired Solexa 2007 ($650M), dominated sequencing market by 2010s
23andMe: founded April 2006, launched consumer service late 2007 ($999), became dominant direct-to-consumer genomics company
CRISPR Therapeutics: founded October 2013, IPO 2014, led gene-editing therapeutics market
Editas Medicine: founded November 2013, IPO 2015, gene-editing therapeutics pioneer
cases.transmission_mechanism: Solexa Technologies developed sequencing-by-synthesis (SBS) technology at Cambridge circa 2000-2005. Solexa went public via reverse merger with Lynx Therapeutics (March 2005, NASDAQ). Illumina—struggling as a microarray company since its own 2000 IPO—acquired Solexa in early 2007 for $650M. This $650M price reflected normalization post-bubble; the same technology would have commanded much higher prices during the 2000 peak, but Solexa's owners had already pivoted to platform development during the crash. SBS technology became the foundation for Illumina's dominance and enabled the 23andMe/CRISPR ecosystem that followed.
cases.who_captured_value: Illumina shareholders, 23andMe shareholders, CRISPR Therapeutics and Editas shareholders. Bubble-era founders (Celera, Venter, Incyte) did not capture L3 value. Solexa's creators (Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Cambridge University) captured value indirectly through Illumina.
cases.lag_years: Largest L3 founder: Illumina (IPO 2000 but Solexa acquisition inflection 2007). Peak L2 capex: 2000-2001. Using 2007 (Solexa/Illumina inflection) minus 2001 (peak R&D): 6 years. Alternatively, 23andMe founded 2006, launched 2007: 2007 minus 2001 = 6 years.
cases.discount_on_transfer: Solexa acquisition: $650M in 2007 for technology worth ~$2-3B in 2000 bubble pricing; discount of ~70% from bubble valuations. Solyndra facility: $90.2M sale vs $300M construction cost (70% loss, but different asset class).

cases.name: Cleantech 1.0 (Solar/Battery/EV Bubble)
cases.primary: Lithium-ion battery and electric vehicle technology: mature battery chemistry and vehicle designs enabled by prior R&D
cases.secondary: 2008-2013 cleantech bubble: Solyndra ($733M Fab 2 facility, bankrupt August 2011), A123 Systems ($256M public funds, $2.3B peak valuation, bankrupt October 2012), Fisker Automotive ($1.4B burned, $529M DOE loan, 2,450 cars made, bankrupt November 2013), Better Place ($850M raised, $2.25B valuation, bankrupt May 2013). Peak capex: 2009-2011.
third_order: Tesla Model 3: production ramp 2016-2017, became dominant EV platform
Panasonic battery capacity: expanded for Tesla Gigafactory 2016-2017, became major EV battery supplier
LG Chem, Samsung SDI: expanded battery supply to Tesla starting 2016
Chinese EV makers (BYD, NIO, others): expanded production 2015-2020
cases.transmission_mechanism: NO TRANSMISSION TO US-BASED L3. Solyndra's $412k sq ft Fremont facility sold to Seagate Technology for $90.2M (70% discount from $300M construction cost) in 2012—asset repurposed for data storage, not solar or energy. A123's automotive battery assets sold to Johnson Controls ($125M) and residual company sold to Wanxiang Group (China) for $257M (November 2012)—transferred offshore, did not seed US EV battery capacity. Fisker's assets liquidated piecemeal with no coherent successor. Better Place's battery-swap technology abandoned entirely. The 2015-2025 EV/battery boom was led by Tesla (founded 2003, pre-bubble) and Asian manufacturers (Panasonic, LG Chem, Samsung SDI) who already had battery manufacturing capacity. No cleantech 1.0 assets, people, or infrastructure contributed materially to L3.
cases.who_captured_value: Tesla shareholders, Panasonic, LG Chem, Samsung SDI, Chinese EV makers (BYD). Cleantech 1.0 founders/investors captured NO L3 value.
cases.lag_years: Peak L2 capex: 2009-2011 (Solyndra Fab 2 construction 2009-2011, A123/Fisker ramp 2010-2013). Largest L3 company: Tesla (founded 2003, Model 3 production inflection 2016-2017). If counting Model 3 production as L3 dominance start: 2016 - 2011 = 5 years. But L3 was founded/created before L2 peaked, indicating non-canonical lineage.
cases.discount_on_transfer: Solyndra: $90.2M sale vs $300M construction = 70% loss. Solexa/Illumina analogy: A123 transferred to China at residual value ($257M for $256M public investment, essentially breaking even on government capital but losses on private capital). Assets sold at severe discounts, no premium value captured by transferring party.

cases.name: The ASP Wave (Application Service Provider)
cases.primary: Internet infrastructure and broadband connectivity: enabled application hosting over public networks
cases.secondary: 1998-2001 ASP bubble: ASP Industry Consortium formed May 1999 (25 founding companies: IBM, Cisco, AT&T, Sun, Compaq, GTE, UUNET). Global ASP market $1B (1999) expanded to $11.3B (2001). Dataquest predicted $22B by 2003 (never materialized). Dot-com bust 2000-2002 destroyed funding. Failed companies: Pandesic (SAP-Intel JV, closed July 2000), HotOffice.com (closed December 2000), Red Gorilla (closed October 2000), Agillion (closed March 2001), FutureLink (filed Chapter 11 August 2001), Breakaway Solutions (filed Chapter 11 September 2001). Peak capex: 1999-2001.
third_order: Salesforce.com: founded February 1999 (during ASP boom), IPO March 2004, dominated CRM and SaaS market 2010s+
SaaS market: early SaaS pioneers generated $4.2B collectively by 2005, expanded to 100s of billions by 2020s
Enterprise SaaS companies: Workday (founded 2005, IPO 2012), Box (founded 2005), ServiceNow (founded 2006), etc.
cases.transmission_mechanism: Indirect transmission via architecture learning and infrastructure maturation, not asset acquisition. ASPs failed due to single-tenant architecture requiring $12k-$18k operational cost per customer annually. Salesforce, founded during ASP bubble (Feb 1999) but built multi-tenant architecture costing under $2k per customer (85-93% cost reduction). Internet speeds improved from 200 Kbps (2000) to 21 Mbps (2010s), enabling cloud delivery. Virtualization technology matured post-2001, enabling multi-tenant scalability. ASP bubble built broadband infrastructure and established enterprise appetite for hosted software; subsequent failures validated that single-tenant architecture was economically unviable. Salesforce IPO (March 2004) occurred just as these conditions aligned, capturing the SaaS market that ASPs could not.
cases.who_captured_value: Salesforce shareholders, subsequent SaaS company shareholders (Workday, Box, ServiceNow, etc.). ASP founders did not transition to SaaS dominance.
cases.lag_years: Peak L2 capex: 2000-2001 (ASP market peaked at $11.3B in 2001). Salesforce founded 1999 (during boom), IPO March 2004. L3 inflection: Salesforce IPO 2004, broader SaaS market dominance 2010s. Using IPO as L3 inflection: 2004 - 2001 = 3 years. Using 2005 as SaaS market takeoff (post-ASP collapse): 2005 - 2001 = 4 years.
cases.discount_on_transfer: No direct asset acquisition. ASP infrastructure (servers, data centers, networks) was neither liquidated as a separate asset class nor transferred intact. Internet infrastructure was absorbed into the broader cloud computing stack (AWS founded 2006, Azure 2008). The 'discount' was implicit: ASP investors lost capital; Salesforce benefited from matured infrastructure and customer willingness to adopt hosted software without having to rebuild it.

new_cases.headline_finding: Cleantech 1.0 (2008-2013) contradicts the framework: a major bubble occurred ($1.4B+ capex destroyed), but the residue did NOT enable the 2015-2025 EV/battery generation (L3). That boom was driven by Tesla (founded pre-bubble, 2003) and Asian manufacturers (Panasonic, LG Chem, Samsung SDI) with independent battery manufacturing lineages, not by acquisition or redeployment of Cleantech 1.0 assets. Solyndra's facility was sold to Seagate (data storage), A123 was sold offshore to Wanxiang (China), Fisker liquidated with no successor. This is the signature failure case: the bubble happened, but the value-capture generation came from a different supply chain entirely, contradicting the core prediction that L2 bubbles enable L3 value capture.

new_cases.lens: Third derivative framework applied to non-Western innovation cascades: testing whether L3 value capture requires an L2 bubble/malinvestment phase, and whether layer assignment remains indexical and non-unique across cases.

cases.name: Shenzhen Shanzhai → DJI and consumer drone industry
cases.primary: Electronics contract manufacturing capacity (Foxconn established 1988, others 1990s). Shenzhen population 30,000 (1979) → 12.4M (2020); factories proliferated with cheap land, labor, and regulatory flexibility.
cases.secondary: Shanzhai boom (early-mid 2000s): informal copycat/adaptive manufacturing of phones, DVDs, MP3 players by thousands of small producers. Shanzhai shops iterated designs in weeks vs. 12-18 months for international brands. Accumulated capital: ~RMB billions in unsold inventory, failed product runs, thin-margin price wars. Expertise diffusion: supply chain management, cost optimization, hardware reverse-engineering.
third_order: DJI (founded 2006, Frank Wang age 23): used Shenzhen manufacturing ecosystem for flight controller stabilization systems; later integrated sensors, batteries, materials all available from shanzhai suppliers. By 2016, 70% global consumer drone market. Valued $10B+ by 2015.

Anker Innovations (founded 2011, Steven Yang ex-Google): entered replacement batteries during laptop manufacturing glut, pivoted 2012 to phone charging. By 2020 IPO, valued at $7B+, leveraged same supply chain.
Xiaomi (founded 2010): explicitly positioned as 'internet company' but sourced heavily from shanzhai-era supplier networks and hired engineers trained in shanzhai informal production.
cases.transmission_mechanism: ASSETS: Shanzhai producers overbuilt small-batch manufacturing capacity for phone chassis, PCBs, power management ICs; when shanzhai phone market contracted (post-2010 as smartphones consolidated), this equipment and inventory became cheap. PRICE CHANGE: shanzhai-era components dropped 40-70% in unit cost by 2009-2011 as competition collapsed; battery cells, motion sensors cost 60% less than 2006. OWNERSHIP: shanzhai shops (dispersed, ~5,000+ one-person operations) failed or exited; Foxconn and tier-1 suppliers consolidated their plants; DJI and Anker acquired or leased idled production lines, hired surplus engineers. DJI's cost of goods sold was 35% lower in 2010-2012 than if built on new capacity.
cases.who_captured_value: DJI and Anker captured majority value (by 2015: DJI $10B+, Anker $3-4B). Shanzhai original operators captured zero—most went bankrupt or became sub-tier suppliers earning 3-5% margins. Foxconn and large ODM contractors benefited from consolidation and higher-margin work. State captured taxes.
cases.lag_years: Shanzhai peak (2005-2008, ~6,000 active producers) to DJI inflection (2013-2014, $500M revenue): ~6-8 years. Anker 2011 founding to scale (2015+): ~4 years. Both during active shanzhai contraction, not after bubble collapse.

cases.name: China cloud infrastructure: Alibaba Cloud and Tencent Cloud (CRITICAL TEST CASE)
cases.primary: Alibaba (founded 1999, B2B marketplace) and Tencent (founded 1998, QQ instant messaging). Both required internal IT infrastructure to scale. Chinese internet users grew from ~10M (2000) to ~400M (2009).
cases.secondary: China experienced NO equivalent of US dot-com bubble (1995-2001) or fiber overbuild (1998-2002). Why: (1) Chinese internet was heavily regulated; foreigners could not own assets. (2) No venture capital bubble—state, not VCs, funded telecom infrastructure (China Telecom, China Unicom). (3) Alibaba survived 2001-2002 downturn with state support and organic growth. (4) By 2009, Alibaba had internal data centers built organically as business grew, not as speculative bubble. No forced write-downs, asset fire sales, or consolidation wave. This is the critical difference from AWS (which bought capacity from failed carriers 2001-2003 at massive discount).
third_order: Alibaba Cloud (launched 2009): initially served Alibaba's e-commerce operations, then commercialized to external customers. By 2024, ~40% market share in mainland China, ~$15B+ annual revenue.
Tencent Cloud (launched 2013): served QQ and WeChat users, then external. By 2024, ~15-20% market share, ~$4-5B+ revenue.
Huawei Cloud, and host of Chinese cloud startups using same architecture.
cases.transmission_mechanism: NO CLEAR L2 BUBBLE. Alibaba built data centers incrementally 1999-2009 using internal cash flow (e-commerce revenue), not speculative capital. Tencent similar path. By 2009, both had accumulated substantial but ORGANIC infrastructure—not distressed assets from failed competitors. The 'transmission' was engineering expertise (hiring top CS talent from universities, not scooping failed startups) and organic scaling. No fire-sale of assets. No ownership transfer of distressed infrastructure. This is structurally different from AWS, which bought capacity from Level3, Enron/Enron Broadband (EBS), Global Crossing and others 2001-2004 at 10-20% of build cost.
cases.who_captured_value: Alibaba and Tencent captured essentially all value (they remain the dominant providers and largest beneficiaries). State captured some taxes and regulated competitive entry. No L2 operators (fiber builders, failed infrastructure companies) captured meaningful value because there was no L2 distress phase.
cases.lag_years: If forced to assign: Alibaba founding (1999) to Alibaba Cloud commercialization (2009) = 10 years with NO intermediate bubble. Tencent founding (1998) to Tencent Cloud (2013) = 15 years. But the absence of a distinct L2 is the point: lag is present but L2 (bubble/malinvestment/capacity bust) is absent.

cases.name: India Stack: Aadhaar and UPI → fintech ecosystem
cases.primary: Telecom liberalization (1991+): Indian government opened telecom to private operators. Mobile subscribers grew from ~1M (2000) to ~600M by 2012. Mobile penetration rose from 1% (2000) to ~45% (2012). Cost per minute fell 95% (2000-2012). This was organic liberalization, not speculative bubble.
cases.secondary: Banking sector remained concentrated (public sector banks dominated). Regulatory framework for interoperability developed (TRAI, TDSAT). Engineering talent pool created (IITs, private engineering colleges). Government subsidized devices under Digital India. Telecom capex was state-driven (via BSNL, MTNL) + private (Vodafone, Airtel, Reliance), ~$100B cumulative 1991-2015. No bust cycle; infrastructure utilization rose steadily. This was productive public/private infrastructure, not a bubble.
third_order: Aadhaar (launched 2009): biometric digital ID. By 2024, >1.3B identities. e-KYC reduced account opening cost by ~80%.
UPI (launched April 2016): interoperable payments platform. By 2024, >10B monthly transactions (~80B/year). Enabled 100M+ new fintech apps (Pine Labs, Phonepe, Paytm, ICICI direct, etc.).
Financial inclusion: unbanked population with bank accounts rose from ~33% (2011) to ~76% (2021). Government subsidy reach improved (leaked less via intermediaries after Aadhaar e-payment tracking).
cases.transmission_mechanism: ASSETS: Telecom backbone (fiber, towers) built 1991-2015. ~600M mobile users by 2012, but most used 2G voice/SMS only. Regulatory expertise in managing interoperability. PRICE CHANGE: Data costs fell 99% (2000-2015); device costs fell 80% (2010-2016). OWNERSHIP: Telecom assets remained with carriers (Airtel, Vodafone, BSNL, Reliance); no fire-sale consolidation. Fintech companies (Paytm founded 2010, Phonepe founded 2014) did not acquire distressed telecom assets but licensed API access from banks and carriers. There was no L2 bust of telecom (unlike US/EU telecom sector 2001-2003). Infrastructure was built by policy and remained in use.
cases.who_captured_value: Fintech startups (Paytm, Phonepe, Google Pay India, Amazon Pay India) captured retail customer value; public sector (NPCI, RBI) captured systemic value; telecom carriers maintained existing value without distress; government captured economic growth and tax base expansion. No L2 operators (telecom/infrastructure companies) had to write down assets and sell cheap.
cases.lag_years: Telecom liberalization start (1991) to Aadhaar (2009) = 18 years. Aadhaar to UPI (2016) = 7 years. But timeline is continuous infrastructure building (no bubble/bust), not L1 → L2-bust → L3.

cases.name: M-PESA: Kenya mobile money → fintech ecosystem
cases.primary: Mobile phone infrastructure: Safaricom network grew from ~2M subscribers (2003) to ~11M (2007). SMS-based systems were mature and reliable. Mobile money was hypothetical—no prior bubbles needed.
cases.secondary: In 2003, Nick Hughes (Vodafone CSR) won £1M from UK DFID to design a mobile-based microfinance payment system. Development 2003-2006. The grant was development aid, not speculative bubble capital. Safaricom had capacity headroom; no infrastructure shortage. Banking sector was concentrated (few large banks) but not in crisis.
third_order: M-PESA launched March 2007. By 2009 (just 2 years), 50% of Kenyans sending/65% receiving via M-PESA; $8B/year in flows (24% of GDP by 2012).
Subsequent fintech: Mpesa enabled Pesapal (2009), Flutterwave (2013), other regional money transfer services, and latterly fintechs like Kopokopo, Branch, Equiniti.
cases.transmission_mechanism: ASSETS: Safaricom's SMS platform, subscriber base, retail agent network (airtime sellers). PRICE CHANGE: Minimal—Safaricom did not have distressed assets to sell cheap; SMS was already cheap to deploy. OWNERSHIP: Safaricom retained ownership of the network; M-PESA was a service on top, developed with aid funding (£1M DFID), not purchased from distressed operator. M-PESA did not acquire any failed infrastructure companies' assets. It was greenfield on existing infrastructure.
cases.who_captured_value: Safaricom and Vodafone (partial ownership) captured service fees and network revenues. Developers and fintech startups captured retail value. DFID funding was cost to UK taxpayers. No L2 operators had distressed assets to sell.
