cases.lag_years: Mobile infrastructure build (2000-2003) to M-PESA launch (2007) = ~7 years, but continuous growth with no bust. No distinct L2 bubble phase identified.

cases.name: Brazil Pix: Central bank infrastructure → fintech ecosystem
cases.primary: Brazil's existing banking system: ~5,000 ATMs (2010), concentrated among 5-6 large banks (Caixa, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Itau, Santander). Traditional payment rails were expensive and slow (3-5 day transfers). System was stable but inefficient.
cases.secondary: No financial crisis or bubble in this period (2008 crisis had passed; Brazilian economy stable 2009-2019 pre-COVID). Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) began modernization initiative ~2015. No forced asset sales or infrastructure consolidation. No telecom bubble parallel. Decision to build Pix was regulatory modernization and competition policy, not response to crisis.
third_order: Pix launched November 16, 2020 (by BCB decree). By end 2024: 168M users, 64B transactions/year. Enabled ~1,000+ fintech apps (Nu Bank valued $30B by 2024, acquired ~50% of users via Pix; others: Banco Inter, Nubank competitors).
Adoption was fastest in world: ~60% of adult population in 2 years (vs. India UPI ~3 years, Europe SEPA Instant ~5 years).
cases.transmission_mechanism: ASSETS: BCB's existing infrastructure (payment clearinghouses, real-time gross settlement (RTGS) system), banking regulations, central bank balance sheet. Pix was built ON TOP of this, not by acquiring distressed banking assets. PRICE CHANGE: No asset fire-sale; existing banking infrastructure was repurposed/upgraded for Pix (marginal cost). OWNERSHIP: Central bank and commercial banks retained all assets; no transfers from failing operators. Fintech companies licensed into the Pix system as 'payment service providers' (PSP) but did not acquire banking infrastructure.
cases.who_captured_value: Fintechs (Nu Bank $30B, Banco Inter $1B+) captured majority customer value. BCB captured regulatory/systemic control. Commercial banks lost some revenue share but did not face distress. No L2 operators (failed banks or consolidation wave) had assets to sell cheap.
cases.lag_years: Banking system modernization (2015~) to Pix launch (2020) = 5 years. Pix to fintech scale (2022-2024) = 2-3 years. Continuous policy-driven development, no bubble/bust.

cases.name: Brazil ethanol: Government industrial policy and the role of prior sugar capacity
cases.primary: Sugarcane production in Brazil (established centuries prior, especially 1960s-1970s expansion). Sugar was major commodity export. Land, agricultural expertise, mills existed.
cases.secondary: Proálcool mandate (November 14, 1975, via Decree 76,593): Government required ethanol blending in gasoline (response to 1973 OPEC oil shock and Brazil's oil import dependency). Massive government investment in distilleries, agronomic research, engine R&D (1975-1989, ~$10B+ cumulative in 1975 dollars). By mid-1980s, ~400,000 hectares under ethanol sugarcane, capacity built from ~1.4B liters/year (1975) to ~11B liters/year (1989). This was state-directed industrial policy, not speculative bubble. However: in 1980s, oil prices fell; Proálcool became uneconomical and was scaled back (1989-1990). Substantial overcapacity built, then idled. This resembles an L2 'productive bubble' or malinvestment.
third_order: Modern ethanol companies (1990s+): Cosan (founded 1997), Raízen (formed 2011 via merger), Vale Fertilizantes, and ~400 independent mills. Leveraged idle Proálcool-era distillery capacity and agricultural knowledge.

By 2024: Brazil produces ~30B liters/year ethanol; world's 2nd largest producer (after USA), largest exporter. Ethanol cost: ~$0.30-0.40/liter (world's cheapest). Sugar-ethanol industry employs ~1M people.
cases.transmission_mechanism: ASSETS: Proálcool-era distilleries, agricultural research infrastructure, trained workforce, 400k hectares of productive sugarcane land. PRICE CHANGE: Distillery capacity built for ~$300-500M (1975-1989, per unit) became stranded 1986-1990 as oil prices fell; resale/leasing values dropped ~50% by 1992-1995. OWNERSHIP: Initially state-owned or state-subsidized; by late 1980s, some mills were privatized or leased to private operators. In 1990s-2000s, private companies (Cosan, others) acquired or leased distilleries at steep discounts (40-60% of replacement cost) and expanded into integrated sugar-ethanol production.
cases.who_captured_value: Modern ethanol companies (Cosan, Raizen, independents) captured margin value by acquiring low-cost distillery assets post-1990. State lost via write-downs and subsidy cessation. Farmers benefited from sustained demand. Exported economy benefited. End consumers (fuel buyers) benefited from low-cost ethanol.
cases.lag_years: Proálcool start (1975) to peak overexpansion (1989) to consolidation wave (1992-2000) to modern scale-up (2000+). Peak-capex 1989 to modern company founding ~1997 (Cosan) = ~8 years. This is consistent with L2 → L3 lag. However, the causation is ambiguous: were modern companies enabled by cheap distillery assets, or would they have entered anyway (given rising oil prices post-1999)? Evidence quality medium because oil-price confound.

new_cases.headline_finding: The framework's necessity claim is CONTRADICTED by three major non-Western cases (China cloud, India Stack, M-PESA, Brazil Pix). All built hyperscale L3 systems WITHOUT preceding L2 bubbles/malinvestment/asset fire-sales. Instead, L3 was enabled by: (1) organic infrastructure build (telecom liberalization), (2) policy-driven modernization (Pix), or (3) venture backing on virgin ground (M-PESA). China cloud is the sharpest test: Alibaba and Tencent accumulated substantial infrastructure 1998-2009 via internal cash flow, not speculative bubble. No equivalent of US dot-com/fiber bust. Alibaba Cloud commercialization (2009+) did NOT acquire distressed carrier assets as AWS did (Level3, Global Crossing, 2001-2004). The Brazilian ethanol case partially supports the framework (Proálcool overcapacity did enable modern producer entry), but is confounded by rising oil prices post-1999. Shenzhen Shanzhai is ambiguous: shanzhai boom was not a clear 'bust' (many producers persisted or merged into tier-1), and DJI/Anker were founded DURING the boom (2006/2011), not after a collapse. The operator framework is thus at best SUFFICIENT but NOT NECESSARY for L3 emergence in non-Western contexts. The assignment's core warning is validated: layer assignment remains indexical (shanzhai is both L2-for-DJI AND L1-for-mass-production-of-phones). When no true L2 bubble occurs, calling the process 'L1-L2-L3' becomes post-hoc and loses predictive power.

new_cases.lens: Third-order value capture: L1 innovation enables L2 reorganisation (institutional, human, or capacity) which then enables L3 businesses to capture most value. Focus on human-capital and organizational-capital channels (not just physical asset bubbles) and transmission mechanisms at the asset and ownership level.

cases.name: German Synthetic Dyes to Pharmaceuticals and Haber-Bosch
cases.primary: Perkin's aniline dye synthesis (1856) enables industrial synthetic dye production, displacing natural dyes
cases.secondary: BASF (founded 1865, major lab investment 1870s-1890s), Bayer (founded 1863, Elberfeld labs), Hoechst (founded 1863) systematize research as institutional innovation. Cost per unit synthetic dye falls 10-100x; German firms capture >90% global dye production by 1880s.
third_order: Aspirin: Bayer synthesizes acetylsalicylic acid and patents aspirin (1899) using dye-lab research capability
Haber-Bosch nitrogen fixation: BASF with Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch develop ammonia synthesis (1909) for fertilizers and explosives, using same systematized research infrastructure
Pharmaceutical dominance: German chemical firms dominate global pharma, fertilizers, and explosives through 1930s
cases.transmission_mechanism: Asset: Institutional research laboratory capability (PhD scientists, experimental methods, patent generation system). Price change: Cost of dye production fell 10-100x (1870s-1890s); German firms captured 90%+ global production and premium patent position. Ownership before: Scattered academic chemistry. Ownership after: Concentrated in BASF, Bayer, Hoechst labs (no asset transfer between firms; same firms redeployed lab capacity to pharmaceuticals and nitrogen fixation). Critical: The research lab was an overbuild initially (capacity exceeded dye market demand by 1890s) but proved redeployable to adjacent high-value domains.
cases.who_captured_value: BASF, Bayer, Hoechst shareholders. BASF alone: ~5M Marks revenue (1865) to ~100M Marks (1914); pharmaceutical and nitrogen-fixation business dominated corporate value by 1914.
cases.lag_years: 1899 (Aspirin patent) - 1880s (peak BASF/Bayer lab investment) = ~20 years; 1909 (Haber-Bosch patent) - 1880s = ~25-30 years
cases.discount_on_transfer: No asset transfer; same firms captured both L2 and L3 value. No discount applicable.
sources: Homburg, Ernst. The Transformation of the German Chemical Industry by World War I (2004)
Murmann, Johann Peter. Knowledge and Competitive Advantage (2003)
Willcocks, J.C. The Manufacture of Organic Chemicals (1921)

cases.name: Nokia Mobile Phone Collapse to Supercell (Finnish Gaming)
cases.primary: Nokia dominates mobile phone market (1990s-2007): 40% market share, $250B market cap (2000). Enables Finnish electronics and telecom employment concentration.
cases.secondary: iPhone disruption (2007). Nokia strategic failure: partnership with Microsoft on Windows Phone (2011) instead of Android. Market share collapse: 40% (2007) to 3% (2013). Layoffs: 60,000+ employees 2008-2013, concentrated in Espoo and Helsinki, including deep mobile systems and optimization engineers.
third_order: Supercell: Founded 2010, Clash of Clans (2012) massive hit, $1.6B revenue (2016), $10.2B acquisition by Tencent (2016), IPO 2023 ~$40B valuation
Remedy Entertainment: Founded 1995, grew post-2010 (later acquired by Take-Two 2021 for $305M)
Note: Rovio (Angry Birds 2009) founded 2003 predates Nokia collapse, weakens causal attribution
cases.transmission_mechanism: Asset: Laid-off Nokia engineers with deep mobile systems optimization, embedded systems, real-time network protocols expertise. Price change: Market wage for systems engineers/software architects fell (Finland labor surplus 2010-2013); estimated 10-30% wage compression vs. 2007 levels. Ownership before: Nokia corporate employment. Ownership after: Individual engineers as free agents (post-layoff 2010-2013). Supercell recruited ex-Nokia personnel into founding/early teams (plausible but weakly documented in public record). Critical: Timing is very short (2-4 years), violating framework expectation of 30+ year lags.
cases.who_captured_value: Supercell founders (Ilkka Paananen and team), early employees, Tencent (51% stake 2016). By 2023 IPO, value ~$40B mostly to Tencent.
cases.lag_years: Supercell founding (2010) - Nokia peak capex/employment (2007) = 3 years; Clash of Clans hit (2012) - end of major layoffs (2013) = near-simultaneous or negative lag
cases.discount_on_transfer: Estimated 10-30% wage compression for laid-off engineers 2010-2013 due to labor surplus; unknown
sources: Supercell corporate history and Tencent investor disclosures
Nokia annual reports and press releases (2008-2013)
TechCrunch, Business Insider reporting on Supercell founding (2010-2012)

cases.name: Unit 8200 to Israeli Cybersecurity Industry
cases.primary: Unit 8200 formed (1952) within Israeli Defense Force as signals intelligence unit. Recruits elite mathematical and engineering talent via mandatory military service. Develops deep expertise in cryptography, code-breaking, network reconnaissance.
cases.secondary: Continuous operation and capability development (no collapse or overbuild event). Demobilization: soldiers complete 3-4 year service and exit to civilian tech sector. Repeated talent drain creates consistent supply of ex-8200 founders and early employees to civilian tech.
third_order: Check Point Software: Founded 1993 by Gil Shwed (ex-IDF Signals Corps), core team included Unit 8200 alumni; NASDAQ IPO (1996), market cap $20-30B
Wiz: Founded 2020 by Assaf Rappaport (publicly identified as ex-Unit 8200); $10B+ valuation (2021-2023)
Israeli cybersecurity sector: $6-7B annual exports (2020s); dozens of firms with Unit 8200 lineage (Imperva, SailPoint, others)
cases.transmission_mechanism: Asset: PURE HUMAN CAPITAL - expertise in cryptography, signals processing, network analysis, code-breaking, signals intercept theory. Price change: NOT an asset price change; Israeli cybersecurity exports grew 10-20x (1995-2020). Ownership before: Individual engineers employed by Israeli military. Ownership after: Individual engineers owned their own expertise; founded or joined civilian startups. No physical asset transferred; no classic bubble or overcapacity event. This is steady-state demobilization, not crisis-driven.
cases.who_captured_value: Founders and early employees of Check Point (~$20-30B market cap), Wiz ($10B+ unicorn), and dozens of other Israeli cybersecurity firms. Israeli VC ecosystem and employees captured billions in equity.
cases.lag_years: Check Point founded (1993) - Unit 8200 formation (1952) = 41 years; but 'peak capex' is undefined (continuous operation, not ended). Suggest instead: Check Point IPO (1996) - peak Unit 8200 activity (1980s-1990s overlap) = mechanism is ongoing, not time-bound.
cases.discount_on_transfer: No discount on transfer; human capital not sold, only demobilized. Competitive advantage derived from credibility and peer network, not fire-sale pricing.
sources: Check Point IPO filings and SEC 10-K (1996 onward)
Wiz funding rounds and valuations (Crunchbase, PitchBook 2020-2023)
Israeli news: Globes, The Marker (Unit 8200 linkage to tech sector)
Bessemer Venture Partners Cybersecurity Insights reports

cases.name: Energiewende Renewable Overbuild: Overcapacity Without L3
cases.primary: German Renewable Energy Sources Act (2000) establishes feed-in tariffs: above-market prices guaranteed for renewable generation. Policy shock drives renewable targets: ~5% (2000) to >20% by 2020.
cases.secondary: Massive subsidized overbuild (2010-2016): Solar PV capacity 4GW (2010) to 40GW (2016); wind 27GW (2010) to 50GW (2016). Grid infrastructure designed for steady baseload + demand-responsive generation, not uncontrollable negative-price spikes. Result: Wholesale electricity spot price goes negative (2012-2016), bottoming -500 EUR/MWh (2016).
third_order: Expected L3 candidates - all contradicted or null:
Battery storage (Tesla Powerwall 2015, Eos Energy Devices) - global phenomenon not uniquely enabled by Energiewende; deployment not concentrated in Germany
Grid demand-response startups - emerged but remain niche ($1-5B market cap max), not comparable to semiconductor/internet scale
Power-to-X (green hydrogen, synthetic fuels) - emerged post-2015 but unclear if negative prices enabling (still require subsidies)
Electrified transport (Tesla EVs, others) - not German companies, not uniquely enabled by Energiewende
cases.transmission_mechanism: Asset: Excess renewable generation capacity (owned by utilities, farmers, cooperatives, cooperatives) + grid infrastructure (state/regulated). Price change: Wholesale electricity spot price becomes negative (-500 EUR/MWh 2016) when generation exceeds demand (typical: 4am solar peak, low demand). Ownership before: Grid designed for baseload. Ownership after: Grid receives uncontrollable negative-price supply spikes. Critical problem: who benefited? Industrial electricity consumers got cheap power temporarily, but renewable producers HARMED (forced to sell at negative prices, destroying ROI on $200B+ installed capacity 2010-2016).
cases.who_captured_value: Industrial electricity consumers (temporary price benefit). Possibly energy-intensive manufacturers relocated to Germany post-2012 (attracted by cheap power) but no documented new German manufacturing clusters attribute causation to negative prices. Siemens, ABB (existing grid companies) captured incremental value from balancing infrastructure, not new L3 firms.
cases.lag_years: No L3 firm emerged. Overcapacity (L2) 2010-2016 did not enable new-industry formation (L3). Lag is undefined or infinite.
cases.discount_on_transfer: Negative prices destroyed value for renewable generators: $200B+ installed capacity (2010-2016) saw returns compressed or negative 2012-2016. Instead of asset transfer enabling L3, asset value destruction occurred without corresponding new-industry emergence.
sources: Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems. Electricity production from solar and wind in Germany (annual reports 2010-2016)
European Power Exchange (EPEX) Spot market data and reports (2010-2016)
Agora Energiewende. German electricity market in 2016 (2017)
Bruegel Institute. The economic and geopolitical implications of renewable energy (multiple reports)

new_cases.headline_finding: The framework's causal mechanism works for HUMAN-CAPITAL channels (Unit 8200, German dyes research labs, Nokia engineers) but fails for PURE CAPACITY OVERBUILD without complementary institutional recipients (Energiewende). The framework also requires much shorter lags for labor-market adjustments in small open economies (Nokia: 2-5 years) than for physical asset deployment (electricity: 30+ years, or absent). Unit 8200 case reveals a critical revision: the framework does NOT require L2 to fail or crash; pure demobilization of human capital from a standing institution can drive L3 value capture without any financial distress event, suggesting the causal mechanism is about capability redeployment, not bubbles.

new_cases.lens: Testing the sufficiency of overbuild (L2) alone for third-order value capture (L3). Control cases where massive capacity expansion occurred but no transformative commercial recombination emerged. Framework predicts that overbuild without property-rights transfer, price discovery, free entry, and asset liquidation will fail to generate L3. Hypothesis: the missing ingredient across null cases is the absence of ownership transfer and labor/capital mobility with equity participation, not merely the presence of overbuild.

cases.name: Soviet Union Military-Industrial Complex
cases.primary: Aerospace and defense technology (ICBMs, radar, electronics manufacturing)
cases.secondary: Redundant parallel production capacity across 1000+ factories and research institutes; defense spending 12-17% of GDP (~$100-150bn annual equivalent peak 1980s)
third_order: None. Post-1991 collapse: assets remained state-owned, no commercial transformation. Closed system prevented spinoffs or new entrants. Worker wage suppression, unemployment, not firm liquidation.
cases.transmission_mechanism: No mechanism exists. Assets could not be sold: (1) no private buyer class outside state; (2) prices suppressed by command economy, preventing cost rationalization or market-clearing; (3) state retained ownership claims; (4) no liquidation or bankruptcy of failed plants or firms. Unlike assembly line (L3 of electricity), which required falling component prices enabling Ford to recombine labor + tools at lower cost, Soviet overcapacity at artificially high real-resource cost enabled no profitable recombination.
cases.who_captured_value: USSR state initially through military output; post-1991 successor states bore losses through unemployment and stranded workers. Vendor-capitalists and military-industrial apparatchiks captured rents during Soviet period; no transfer to innovators or entrepreneurs.
cases.lag_years: N/A: no L3 formation. If counting 1960 (peak Soviet modernization) as L2 start to 1991 (collapse) = 31 years of forbearance without liquidation.
sources: Soviet Defense Spending and Industrial Capacity: Firth & Noren (CIA estimates, 1980s)
Soviet Industrial Overcapacity and Successor-State Asset Stranding: Gaddy & Ickes, Brookings Institution, 1990s analyses

cases.name: Japan's Lost Decade: Asset Bubble & Zombie Forbearance
cases.primary: Miniaturization, precision manufacturing, embedded systems (1960s-1980s boom period)
cases.secondary: Asset bubble 1986-1990: Tokyo office real estate $1.5m/sq meter (1989), Nikkei 38,957 (Dec 1989). Banking cascade into non-performing loans; NPL stock peaked ~40% of bank assets by mid-1990s. Cumulative overbuild in real estate, equities, and subsidiary holdings via keiretsu cross-leverage.
third_order: Minimal emergence. Foreign M&A acquirers <2% of M&A value until 2000s (no L3 entrants).
Keiretsu structures and lifetime employment norms prevented spinoff generation and talent redeployment.
Incumbent corporations and banks retained zombie subsidiary holdings through forbearance (1992-2005).
Credit continued to firms with ROA < cost of debt; losses recognized slowly, borne by workers via wage stagnation not firm liquidation.
cases.transmission_mechanism: Blocked. Successful cases (US S&L crisis 1980s → commercial real estate liquidation at 10-30¢ on dollar → venture-backed recovery 1990s) required asset transfer. Japan: Bank of Japan and Ministry of Finance directed continued credit to zombies; collateral never marked to market; ownership never transferred from keiretsu holders to new acquirers. No recombination mechanism existed because assets remained under original owners at artificially supported prices.
cases.who_captured_value: Incumbent banks (Sumitomo, Mitsubishi UFJ, etc.) and corporations (Toyota, Sony, etc.) through delayed loss recognition and forbearance; workers bore costs via wage suppression and lifetime employment obligations becoming liabilities; VC formation never recovered, so no L3 entrants captured upside.
cases.lag_years: 1995 (peak forbearance policy) to 2005-2010 (stagnation continued); 10-15 years without liquidation. No L3 founding date (emergence never occurred).
cases.discount_on_transfer: Unknown (no transfers occurred; forbearance policy prevented market pricing)
sources: Japan's Lost Decade and Zombification: Peek & Rosengren, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, 1990s-2000s
Main Bank System and Forbearance: Aoki & Patrick, Columbia University, late 1990s analyses
Japanese Venture Capital: Hiroyuki Odagiri, comparative study showing VC formation lag 1990-2005

cases.name: European 3G Mobile Licenses: Regulated Spectrum Overbuild
cases.primary: GSM mobile technology and UMTS standard (1980s-1990s development)
cases.secondary: License auctions 2000-2001: ~EUR 120-140bn aggregate (Germany EUR 46.8bn, UK GBP 22.5bn, France EUR 30bn, Italy EUR 9bn, Spain EUR 12bn). Network buildout capex: additional EUR 200-300bn (2000-2006). Total L2: EUR 350-450bn. Over-dimensioned networks built for demand forecasts that never materialized.
third_order: Partial, contested emergence. Vodafone captured some value via international M&A arbitrage (license-cost differentials); Deutsche Telekom remained state-influenced, never achieved ROIC targets.
France Télécom loaded with debt, divested Wanadoo ISP at loss. Smaller entrants (3, Telenor) entered but margins compressed.
Stranded capex: Over-built 3G networks remained in incumbent balance sheets 15+ years; no repurposing.
cases.transmission_mechanism: Blocked by regulation and asset structure. Electricity (L1) → Factory electrification (L2) → Assembly line (L3): prices fell (Edison/GE from $0.30/kWh to $0.05), enabling Ford/GM to acquire and recombine at profit. 3G: Spectrum non-tradeable across countries; prices never market-cleared; regulator-capped termination rates and roaming prevented price discovery. Incumbent owners (Deutsche Telekom, France Télécom, BT) retained assets; no liquidation; IPP entrants built natural gas plants instead of acquiring 3G capacity. Asset immobility: spectrum cannot be repurposed across borders or industries.
cases.who_captured_value: Mobile incumbents retained market share but margins compressed. Spectrum-owning governments captured one-time auction fees (~EUR 120bn), then saw asset values stagnate. Users captured value through penetration (5% → 100% of population) and nominal price decline 50%, but operators' ROI remained modest. Vendors (Ericsson, Alcatel) captured equipment sales but not ownership upside.
cases.lag_years: License auctions 2000-2001 (peak capex year). No L3 founding of note (incumbent-operated networks do not count as new L3 recombination). 2000 to 2010+ = 10+ years without transformation.
cases.discount_on_transfer: N/A (no significant secondary-market spectrum transfer occurred within Europe during this window; Vodafone's value capture came from consolidating multiple incumbents' networks, not from buying distressed assets)
sources: EU Telecom Auction Data: European Commission (2000-2002 reports)
3G Financial Performance: Analysys Mason, Frost & Sullivan reports (2005-2010) on telecom capex and stranded investment
Regulatory Price Caps: OECD Telecom Regulation Indicators (2000-2010) showing termination rate suppression

cases.name: Route 128 vs Silicon Valley: Labor Mobility as Differentiator
cases.primary: Semiconductor and integrated circuit design (Bell Labs/Shockley/fairchildren, 1947-1957)
cases.secondary: Minicomputer specialization (Route 128: DEC established 1957, grew to 100k+ employees; closed architecture, proprietary designs, lifetime employment). Silicon Valley: Horizontal specialization (Intel, Fairchild, modular designs, high job mobility, VC formation 1958+). Both regions had minicomputer L2 overbuild by 1970s-1980s.
third_order: Silicon Valley: YES. PCs/workstations (Apple 1976, Sun 1982) emerged using spinoff engineers + VC capital. Fairchild → Intel, AMD, LSI Logic, etc. recombination enabled IBM-compatible PC ecosystem.
Route 128: NO. DEC/Data General failed to pivot to PCs; minicomputer decline in 1980s; cluster dissolved. IBM (outsider, not DEC-derivative) captured PC market.
cases.transmission_mechanism: Silicon Valley: Low-cost Fairchild/Intel engineer talent (spinoffs, founders could retain equity) + Draper's 1958 VC fund → PC/workstation startups acquired/imitated minicomputer reliability at 10x lower cost. Engineers' skills transferred to assemblers (Apple, Compaq) at <50% wages, recombined with new supply chains. Route 128: DEC engineers locked in closed org (lifetime employment norm, no equity spinoff rights); minicomputer proprietary designs (COBOL, PDP-11, VMS) not transferable; no VC exit paths. PCs/workstations developed OUTSIDE Route 128 (IBM, Intel in SV). Asset/knowledge: minicomputer engineering expertise was non-transferable under DEC's employment model; spinoff generation never happened.
cases.who_captured_value: Silicon Valley: Founders (Jobs, Wozniak, McNealy), early investors (Draper, Gaither), 2nd/3rd-gen entrepreneurs (Ellison @ Oracle). Route 128: IBM (PC market), later Intel/AMD (processors) — but NOT Route 128 incumbents (DEC shareholders captured declining value; employees captured wages but not equity upside).
cases.lag_years: SV: Fairchild peak capex/minicomputer boom ~1970; Apple founded 1976, Sun founded 1982 = 6-12 year lag. Route 128: DEC peak ~1970s, decline began early 1980s, collapse by 1990s = no L3, 20-year forbearance before liquidation (DEC acquired by Compaq 1998 at distressed prices).
cases.discount_on_transfer: SV talent redeployment: engineers at 50-70% of Fairchild/DEC wages, but with startup equity compensation. Apple/Compaq/Sun wafer fabs and designs acquired/imitated at <50% of R&D cost (learning curve, shared open IP). Route 128: DEC's Compaq acquisition (1998) at steep discount; DEC liquidated, not recombined.
sources: AnnaLee Saxenian, Regional Advantage (1994), Oxford University Press. Definitive comparison of cluster trajectories.
Fairchild Semiconductor Spinoff Genealogy: multiple academic studies (e.g., Helms, 2008) documenting 20+ major spinoffs
DEC corporate history: Edgar Schein (1997), organizational culture analysis; DEC's later decline well-documented in business press

cases.name: Nuclear Power Plant Overcapacity: Regulated Utility Stagnation
cases.primary: Nuclear fission reactor design and LWR standardization (1960s; Westinghouse, GE, Combustion Engineering)
cases.secondary: US nuclear buildout 1970-1985: 50 GW capacity (from 5 GW in 1970). Cumulative capex ~$150-200bn nominal (1970-1985, ~$500bn+ 2005 dollars). Three Mile Island (1979) triggered regulatory delays (2-5 years per project) and safety-driven cost escalation. Average cost per MW: ~$3-4bn (2005 dollars). 100+ plants built; many never achieved planned utilization due to public resistance.
third_order: Absent/minimal emergence. Utilities (Duke Energy, Commonwealth Edison, Southern Company) retained and operated plants at stable 5-8% ROE (not venture returns).
Independent power producers (1990s+) built natural gas plants, not new nuclear. No new business model emerged from existing overcapacity.
Stranded cost recovery: Utilities sought regulator-guaranteed cost recovery; assets never liquidated or transferred to new operators. 30+ plant projects cancelled; overcapacity written off.
cases.transmission_mechanism: Blocked by regulation and asset structure. Electricity (L1: generators) → Factory electrification (L2: shop-floor adoption) → Assembly line (L3: Ford/GM recombination of labor + modular tools) worked because: prices fell (GE/Westinghouse generators $0.30 → $0.05/kWh); generation separated from adoption; modular equipment. Nuclear: prices ROSE (1970s-80s, +200% due to regulation); generation NOT separated (utilities did both); plants integrated single-purpose assets, not modular or convertible. Stranded 100+ MW capacity for demand that never materialized could not be repurposed or sold at profitable prices.
cases.who_captured_value: Utilities and shareholders: rate-based regulation guaranteed ~5-7% ROE (cost recovery); modest value capture. Vendors (Westinghouse, GE, Bechtel): engineering and construction fees. Public: bore costs through higher electricity rates and subsidies. No new entrants or L3 entrepreneurs captured upside.
cases.lag_years: Peak nuclear capex 1975-1980 (avg $30bn/year). New reactor orders effectively ceased after TMI 1979. 2000-2010 = 20-30 years of stagnation under rate regulation, no L3 emergence.
cases.discount_on_transfer: N/A (no significant secondary-market transfer). Seabrook, Shoreham, Vogtle 1-2 projects either cancelled (sunk cost absorbed by ratepayers) or completed at cost-plus (no discount to new operators).
sources: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) construction cost and licensing delay data (1970-2010)
DOE Cost Analyses and Stranded Cost Recovery: Energy Information Administration, 1990s-2000s reports
Utility Rate Regulation and Nuclear Capex Recovery: FERC and state PUC filings, 1990-2010

new_cases.headline_finding: Overbuild (L2) is necessary but profoundly insufficient for third-order value capture (L3). Across all five control cases—Soviet military-industrial complex, Japan's zombie forbearance, European 3G spectrum auctions, Route 128, and nuclear power—massive capacity expansion occurred without transformative commercial generation. The deciding factor is NOT the scale of investment, but the absence of four coupled mechanisms present in successful cases: (1) clarity of property rights enabling transfer (not state retention or regulatory lock-in), (2) price discovery at or below amortized cost (allowing new acquirers to profit), (3) free entry and spinoff formation by new entrepreneurs with equity ownership (not wage-labor redeployment alone), and (4) actual liquidation or bankruptcy of failed incumbents releasing assets. The Soviet case goes further: overbuild without these mechanisms actively *destroys* value, not merely stagnates. Japan's 15-year forbearance of zombies demonstrates that delaying liquidation extends stagnation, not recovery. The framework's ordinal layer-assignment problem (L3 is always some other case's L1) remains unsolved, but these null cases establish an empirically falsifiable boundary condition: absent property-rights clarity and free entry enabling recombination by new people at new prices, even billion-dollar overbuilds produce no Schumpeterian innovation—only stranded workers and creditors bearing losses.

discriminating_test.verdict_on_framework:
SURVIVES, BUT ONLY AS A NARROW AND RARE SPECIAL CASE — NOT AS A THEORY OF TECHNOLOGICAL SUCCESSION. Three retractions are unavoidable and non-negotiable.

RETRACTION 1 — the ordinal. "Third derivative" as a count of technological generations is not repairable, because in a lattice of converging trajectories (David and Wright's own "technological confluence") the question "which layer is this" has no answer even in principle. The ordinal must be re-anchored on something enumerable: claims on a single named metered capacity. See the reference-frame fix. This costs the operator canonical example (a) outright — under the repaired frame the assembly line is not L3 of electrification, exactly as David and Wright classify it.

RETRACTION 2 — "the bubble made the capacity cheap." Kermani and Ma: cyclical conditions move liquidation recovery rates by only 5-10 percentage points, while fixed physical attributes (mobility, durability, customisation) explain roughly 40% of cross-industry variation. Specificity sets the price; the cycle does not. L2's causal role downgrades from "creates the discount" to "creates the asset in irrational quantity and supplies the cessation event that dislodges it." The discount was always going to be there.

RETRACTION 3 — "usually DIFFERENT PEOPLE." This is false as a general claim and the corpus refutes it repeatedly. Klepper and Simons: 4/4 industries where post-shakeout leaders are early entrants, adjacent diversifiers, or spinoffs of the best early entrants; auto first-cohort exit hazards 76% lower at age 15 and 90% lower at age 25. Chandy and Tellis: ~74% of post-1945 radical innovations from incumbents. In the operator's own example (b), AWS, Google and Netflix are bubble-era firms run by bubble-era people; Salesforce was founded in February 1999 inside the frenzy on identical input prices to the ASPs that died; Illumina was founded April 1998; DJI and Anker were founded during the shanzhai boom; Tesla predates Cleantech 1.0. BASF, Bayer and Hoechst captured both L2 and L3 over 20-30 years with zero change of hands. Insull built the capacity and engineered the demand, and Commonwealth Edison outlived the collapse of its own parent while keeping its customers.

WHAT SURVIVES, RESTATED: A completed, alienable, long-lived capacity built to serve one revenue model can, when that model dies while physical demand for its output survives, be re-priced far below the level any builder could underwrite, and that price reset can make viable a class of downstream business in a DIFFERENT industry that was arithmetically impossible before. The reliable signature is a different COST BASIS, not different people. Value then accrues to whoever holds the cospecialised complement that remains scarce after the input price collapses — which is Teece 1986, and which is usually neither the builder nor the buyer of the asset.

FREQUENCY, STATED HONESTLY: On the ~30 cases assembled across both rounds, roughly 6-8 pass all three necessary conditions, and only about three (Iridium, Interoute/Ebone, post-WWI aviation with a statutory caveat) show value going to a cohort that is genuinely new rather than a recapitalised or lineal survivor. The phenomenon is real and it is roughly a one-in-ten event. It is not a law of how technology creates value. It is one route among at least four, and the corpus contains four hyperscale L3s built with no L2 bust at all (Alibaba/Tencent cloud, India Stack, M-PESA, Brazil Pix).
discriminating_test.the_discriminating_test:
THE TEST, IN ONE SENTENCE: A second-order overbuild produces a third order if and only if the written-down capacity is (i) legally dislodgeable into the operating control of an agent with no sunk commitment to the build, (ii) a general-purpose input to a downstream industry OTHER than the product market the builders were competing in, and (iii) facing surviving physical output demand at the moment the revenue model dies — and the resulting advantage is durable only if (iv) the substrate fraction of the overbuild is large and (v) the real replacement cost of that substrate is not deflating faster than the cost-basis gap can be amortised.

Conditions (i)-(iii) are jointly necessary and, across this corpus, jointly sufficient for a third order to APPEAR. Conditions (iv)-(v) separate a durable third order from a two-year arbitrage. The remaining conditions determine WHO captures and HOW FAST, not WHETHER.

THE MOST IMPORTANT THING THE TEST DOES IS EXCLUDE. If the candidate overbuild is competing output capacity in the market it was built to serve — more solar modules, more airline seats, more radio receivers, more merchant megawatts, more wholesale electricity, more of the same tokens sold to the same buyers — the framework DOES NOT APPLY. In that region Klepper and the Capital Cycle are correct and the framework is wrong: the cull is endogenous, driven by returns to process R&D scaling with output, it requires no bubble at all, and the winners are survivors with a lineage. Forecast consolidation, not succession. The framework's entire domain is the complement of that region: overbuilds whose residue is an INPUT to somebody else's industry. That is why "different people" appears at all in the qualifying cases — not because busts create new cohorts, but because the incumbents are, by construction, in the wrong industry to be the buyers.

SCORING DISCIPLINE. The test is run on a registered frame (see reference_frame_fix), scored PASS/FAIL on each condition before the outcome window opens, with the downstream industry named ex ante at a stated NAICS/SIC level and with a distinct customer set. On the assembled corpus this yields roughly 6-8 passes out of ~30 candidate episodes — Iridium, KPNQwest/Ebone, long-haul fibre into video/CDN, NextWave spectrum, post-WWI airframes into airmail, Brazilian ethanol distilleries (confounded by oil prices), Japanese local loop under mandated unbundling, and marginally Globalstar. Everything else fails on a NAMED condition, and the failures distribute across different conditions rather than piling onto one, which is the property a multi-condition test needs in order not to be a single variable in disguise.

conditions.condition: C1 — ALIENABLE OPERATING CONTROL AT A COST-BASED PRICE. Operating control of the capacity must be capable of moving to an agent with no sunk commitment to the L1/L2 model, by any of at least four instruments: liquidating sale; reorganisation that extinguishes the equity and installs new control; administratively mandated third-party access at cost-based prices; or forced write-down plus control transfer with no insolvency proceeding at all. The operative variable is NOT bankruptcy and NOT legal title — it is forced recognition of loss on the L2 capital plus transferable operating control.
conditions.why_it_matters: This is the condition with the cleanest evidence in the entire programme: it has both a matched pair (same technology, same year, same bust, opposite legal rule, opposite outcome) and a within-case switch (the same country, the same assets, blocked then released by an administrative act). Where control cannot move, capacity that is otherwise perfectly qualified sits fallow for a decade or more. It also correctly reclassifies the Japanese and US telecom cases: US telecom debt was bondholder-held, marked to market, roughly a third of the high-yield index, with no regulatory capital at stake; Japanese exposure sat with undercapitalised banks at book with the minimum capital ratio binding. That is a creditor-structure and accounting question, not a statute question.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Read three documents before the outcome. (1) The licence or permit: does it transfer in insolvency, or does it lapse, revert, or require regulatory re-grant? (2) The security and financing documents: what fraction of the L2 capital is held in mark-to-market instruments (public bonds, securitised debt) versus by prudentially regulated banks at amortised cost? The prediction is that L3 lag decreases in the first share and increases in the second. (3) The regulatory instrument: is there a statutory open-access, unbundling or common-carriage mechanism that forces third-party use at cost even absent any change of ownership? Score PASS if any one of the four instruments is available.
cases_supporting: FCC v. NextWave, 537 U.S. 293 (2003), 8-1: section 525 of the Bankruptcy Code subordinated spectrum policy, licences moved to Cingular ($1.4bn for 34) and Verizon inside eighteen months. This is a pre-registrable test on a legal document and should replace Cogent as the programme's headline datum.

Iridium: Chapter 11 sale of the completed constellation for $25m against a $5-6bn build (0.4%); Boeing operations at $3.5m/month replacing Motorola at $45m/month; profitable by 2005, $135m free cash flow by 2010.

KPNQwest / Ebone: Dutch faillissement, network physically switched off 3 July 2002, assets to Interoute for about EUR 15m against a EUR 1bn build, sold to GTT in 2018 for $2.3bn. True liquidation, textbook outcome.

Japan DSL: NTT local-loop unbundling mandated with zero change in asset ownership; Yahoo!BB at Y990/month for 8Mbps from September 2001, giving Japan the world's cheapest DSL. Proves the condition must be stated as control/access, not title.

Japan post-2002 as a within-case switch: Program for Financial Revival (October 2002), Resona (2003), IRCJ (April 2003), major-bank NPLs down to 2.9% by March 2005 — blockage released administratively, not judicially, and reallocation resumed.
cases_failing: German and Quam UMTS licences: surrendered without refund in 2002, non-transferable in insolvency, left fallow until the May 2010 re-auction. Same technology and same bust as NextWave, opposite rule, opposite outcome. This pair is the strongest single piece of ex-ante-observable evidence in the programme.

Soviet military-industrial complex 1960-1991: no private buyer class, no price system, no liquidation. Overbuild at artificially high real-resource cost enabled no profitable recombination; 31 years of forbearance, zero L3.

Japan 1990-2002: keiretsu cross-holdings, collateral never marked to market, directed credit to firms with ROA below cost of debt. Note Fukao and Kwon: the exit effect was NEGATIVE — productive SMEs died and zombies lived — so the variable is selection of transfer, not speed of it.

European 3G more broadly: spectrum non-tradeable across borders, regulator-capped termination and roaming prevented price discovery, over-dimensioned networks stayed on incumbent balance sheets 15+ years with no repurposing.

US utility holding companies 1922-1932: a large, textbook Perez frenzy whose physical legacy was redistributed through the same incumbents under new regulation. No third generation, no change of hands. The framework's best-documented counter-case on value capture.

US nuclear under rate-base cost recovery: stranded cost socialised, no market-clearing price, plants not separable from the utility. CONTESTED — see the correction note in the falsification rule; the 1999-2002 merchant consolidation may move this to a qualified PASS.

conditions.condition: C2 — OUTPUT-DEMAND SURVIVAL. Physical demand for the OUTPUT of the capacity must survive, and preferably grow, through and after the cessation event. What dies is the revenue model, not the demand. Where the shock kills output demand itself, the mechanism fails and what you are observing is ordinary fire-sale value destruction.
conditions.why_it_matters: This is the framework's first genuinely ex-ante falsification criterion and it is not indexical to where the analyst starts counting. It is checkable from a single observable series at the time of the bust, and it correctly excludes the case where the fire-sale literature has direct measurements against the framework. Ramey and Shapiro found displaced aerospace capital sold to industry insiders at a 29-40% premium over outsiders, up to roughly 100% for newer machine tools, with real losses measured — precisely the case where output demand genuinely died. Without this gate the framework cannot distinguish itself from Shleifer-Vishny.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Code compound growth in PHYSICAL units of the capacity's output from peak to peak plus five years — bits carried, satellite minutes, MWh dispatched, seat-miles, litres blended, inferences served. Deliberately not revenue: revenue is the thing that dies. Score FAIL on any negative compound physical-output growth. This is one series, published, and available at the time of the bust.
cases_supporting: Long-haul fibre 2001-2006: traffic volumes grew strongly through the crash while implied transport cost fell from roughly $3.66/GB at 1998 transit prices to about $0.03/GB at 2009 CDN prices — the delivery cost of a two-hour film going from a few dollars to about five cents.

Iridium: consumer handset demand died, but maritime, aviation, government and remote-industrial demand for satellite minutes survived and grew; the new management explicitly repositioned onto the surviving demand.
Merchant CCGT: gas-fired generation output grew steadily through the bankruptcies, and the plants continued to run. (This case fails on C3, not C2 — which is the point of a multi-condition test.)
cases_failing: US aerospace 1988-1995: the peace dividend killed output demand outright. Insiders paid the premium, outsiders paid less, and the measured result was allocative loss. The confirming negative for this gate.

Energiewende 2010-2016: German electricity demand was flat to declining while solar went 4GW to 40GW and wind 27GW to 50GW; spot prices went negative, bottoming near -500 EUR/MWh in 2016. Value was destroyed for the generators with no downstream industry created — no storage, no power-to-X, no demand-response firm at scale emerged in Germany.
US nuclear 1975-1985: load growth forecasts near 7%/yr collapsed to 1-2%. Over 30 plant projects cancelled and the completed overcapacity had no growing output demand to absorb it.
Teledesic: no output at all — the constellation was never flown, so the series does not exist.

conditions.condition: C3 — CROSS-MARKET INPUT, NOT SAME-MARKET OUTPUT CAPACITY. The written-down capacity must be a general-purpose input to a downstream industry OTHER than the product market the L2 builders were competing in. Where it is competing output capacity in the same market, reorganisation manufactures zombies functionally identical to bank forbearance and value accrues to survivors.
conditions.why_it_matters: This is the condition that reconciles the framework with Klepper and with the Capital Cycle, and it is the single largest source of exclusion in the corpus. Klepper's four firm-by-firm industries — autos, tyres, TV receivers, penicillin — are ALL same-market output capacity, which is exactly why the survivors won 4/4 and why no bubble was required to produce the cull. The Capital Cycle likewise describes supply in a commodity market. In that structure the only asset is market position, and market position cannot change hands cheaply because nobody outside the market wants it. The framework's domain is the complement. It also explains the US airline anomaly: Chapter 11 there produces congestion that should be statistically indistinguishable from Japanese forbearance, and the 'zombie carrier' complaint is the domestic mirror of Caballero-Hoshi-Kashyap.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Name the downstream industry ex ante, at a stated NAICS or SIC level, with a customer set demonstrably distinct from the L2 builders' customer set. If the buyers of the L3 output are the same buyers the L2 firms were fighting over, score FAIL. WARNING: this condition reintroduces a boundary choice, which is the indexicality problem in a new location. It is only admissible if the boundary is registered in writing before the outcome window opens, and any case scored after the fact is inadmissible as evidence for the framework.
cases_supporting: Fibre transport into video distribution and CDN: transport is an input to an industry with entirely different customers from the carriers' enterprise private-line base. Netflix and Cloudflare are in a different NAICS code from Global Crossing.
Iridium: repositioned from consumer telephony to government, maritime and industrial telemetry — a different customer set entirely from the one Motorola built for.
Post-WWI airframes into airmail carriage: military aviation and mail carriage are different industries, and the statutory bridge (Kelly Act, 2 February 1925) created the downstream demand explicitly.

Brazilian Proalcool distilleries into transport fuel: the blend mandate created demand distinct from the sugar export market the mills were built around. Confounded by post-1999 oil prices; medium evidence only.
cases_failing: Merchant CCGT 1992-2006: roughly $250bn built, $150-200bn destroyed, plants sold from Calpine and Mirant into the SAME wholesale power market. Result: fragmentation across NRG, Aquila, Wisconsin Public Service and Fortistar, no consolidating third generation, acquirers earning utility returns.

1920s radio receiver manufacturing: 600+ makers competing down prices into the same consumer market. RCA, Philco and Zenith won by outlasting rivals through scale, brand and a tube patent moat — not by buying competitors' factories at fire-sale prices. NBC was founded 15 November 1926, during the boom, not after the crash. Pure Klepper.
US airlines post-deregulation: repeated Chapter 11 reorganisations of competing output capacity in the same product market, producing persistent congestion rather than reallocation.
Energiewende: the surplus was more of the same commodity delivered into the same market at the wrong hours.

conditions.condition: C4 — HIGH SUBSTRATE-TO-OVERLAY RATIO. The overbuild's durable, immobile, low-customisation fraction (civil works, rights-of-way, conduit, spectrum, interconnection, structures, transmission) must be large relative to its short-lived, chemistry- or vintage-specific programmable fraction (electronics, tooling, software).
conditions.why_it_matters: This is the condition that REPLACES the retracted 'the bubble made it cheap' claim, and it is the one Kermani and Ma actually license: fixed physical attributes — mobility, durability, customisation — explain roughly 40% of cross-industry variation in liquidation recovery rates, generating recoveries from near 70% in transportation to under 10% in some services, while cyclical conditions move recoveries only 5-10 percentage points. Specificity is first-order; the cycle is second-order. Within any single overbuild this predicts WHICH parts transfer and appreciate in use and which are scrapped.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Decompose the L2 capex at the time of the build into assets with 20-40 year lives and near-zero technical obsolescence versus assets with 3-7 year lives and high customisation. This is recoverable from project-finance models, construction contracts and depreciation schedules. Then predict the split, not the aggregate.
cases_supporting: Long-haul fibre: trenching, conduit and rights-of-way were the great majority of build cost, the strands remained in service, and no new US national long-haul network was built from the late 1990s until roughly 2015-17. That last fact is the single strongest datum in the framework's favour and should replace the '% dark fibre' statistic — the 2.7% figure is a misquoted single-city datapoint and must be struck.
Iridium: the constellation itself was the substrate; ground segment, billing and channel were the overlay and were entirely rebuilt.
Spectrum and rights-of-way generally: maximum durability, zero customisation, and the recovery rates to match.
cases_failing: Cleantech 1.0: Solyndra's CIGS line was pure overlay — chemistry-specific tooling worthless once the chemistry lost. The BUILDING transferred, to Seagate for $90.2m against $300m construction, and was repurposed for data storage. That is the substrate/overlay split working exactly as predicted, and it yielded no solar third generation. A123's automotive assets went to Johnson Controls for $125m and the residual offshore to Wanxiang for $257m.
1920s radio: receiver tooling was overlay, model-specific and obsolete within two seasons.
Fisker: piecemeal liquidation with no coherent successor; nothing in the estate was substrate.

conditions.condition: C5 — RESET PERSISTENCE. The real replacement cost of the capacity must not be deflating faster than the L3's cost-basis advantage can be amortised. As a working threshold: if real replacement cost is falling faster than roughly 5% per year, a distressed acquisition confers no durable advantage, because a greenfield builder five years later has a lower basis than the distressed buyer had on day one.
conditions.why_it_matters: This condition retrodicts Cleantech 1.0's failure ex ante, from a published price series, without hindsight — which is a genuine and rare win for the programme. It also delivers the sharpest prospective discrimination available today. It is the reason semiconductor fabs and accelerator fleets can never generate durable third-order advantage from bust-era acquisition while trenched conduit, rights-of-way and grid interconnection rights can.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Take the ten-year trend in real replacement cost per unit of the capacity — the BUILD cost curve, not the output price curve. Farmer-Lafond and Nagy-Farmer-Bui-Trancik give calibrated error bars for this on a named artefact, which is the one thing that literature genuinely delivers. Score FAIL above roughly 5%/yr real deflation.
cases_supporting: Trenched conduit and rights-of-way: real cost flat to rising, driven by labour and permitting. The 2001 acquirer's basis was still advantaged fifteen years later.
Spectrum: real replacement cost rising. NextWave licences bought out of a 1998 auction default were more valuable, not less, by 2003-05.
Iridium: pre-reusable-launch, constellation replacement cost was flat to rising, so the $25m basis stayed advantaged for over a decade.
Ethanol distillation capacity: slow-deflating, and the 1990s acquirers at 40-60% of replacement cost kept the advantage.
cases_failing: Cleantech 1.0 solar: module prices fell roughly 80% between 2008 and 2012, so any distressed 2011 solar asset was economically obsolete on the day of purchase. This alone is sufficient to predict, ex ante, that the Solyndra residue would seed nothing.
Battery chemistry 2010-2013: A123's LFP-era tooling was overtaken on cost and energy density by NMC and later scaled LFP; the 2012 buyer inherited a depreciating basis.
Semiconductor fabs and DRAM generally: replacement cost per unit of capability deflates faster than any bust-era discount can be amortised.

conditions.condition: C6 — AGGREGABILITY, AND PRICING AS A METERED SERVICE. The written-down capacity must be re-assemblable by one buyer or a small number, AND — critically — the input must be purchasable downstream as a metered service priced off the written-down basis, not only as lumpy title.
conditions.why_it_matters: This condition carries the single most counterintuitive finding in the programme, and it is the one that resolves most of the value-capture confusion. In the best-documented cross-market case, the buyers of the ASSETS earn utility returns while the equity value accrues to firms that bought SERVICES priced off written-down assets. Netflix never bought fibre. Cloudflare never bought fibre. Cogent, Level 3 and Zayo bought the fibre and earn utility returns on it. The mechanism must therefore be restated as INPUT-PRICE RESET, not asset transfer. Where the capacity is only saleable as lumpy title and cannot be metered, fragmentation follows and no consolidating third generation appears.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Count separable parcels and ask whether a natural aggregator exists. Then ask the decisive question: can a downstream firm buy a metered unit of this capacity — a Mbps-month, a satellite-minute, a MWh, a GPU-hour — at a price set by the written-down basis, without buying the asset? If the answer is no, expect fragmentation and utility returns.
cases_supporting: IP transit and colocation post-2001: metered, priced off extinguished capital structures, and consumed by Netflix and Cloudflare who never touched the underlying assets.

Cogent: aggregated assets from 13 failing carriers 2001-04, roughly $14bn book value for about $60m — the aggregator role played, though Cogent itself was founded in 1999 and is a bubble-era firm, not a post-crash vulture.
Interoute/Ebone: a single indivisible network, one buyer, EUR 15m in, $2.3bn out to GTT in 2018.
Iridium: an indivisible constellation vertically integrated with the service, which is the rare case where asset owner and value capturer coincide.
cases_failing: Merchant CCGT: plants dispersed across NRG, Aquila, Wisconsin Public Service, Fortistar and local utilities at 15-50% of book depending on vintage and location. No single third-generation entrant captured the spread; the corpus records this explicitly as fragmented rather than concentrated capture.

Energiewende: generation dispersed across utilities, farmers and cooperatives, with negative prices harming the owners and no metered mechanism by which a downstream industry could contract off the written-down basis.
1920s radio manufacturing: tooling dispersed across hundreds of failing shops with no aggregator and no metered input.

conditions.condition: C7 — RECOMBINATION PERMISSION IN THE LABOUR MARKET. Where the residue is human rather than physical, the cessation must release operators into a jurisdiction whose law and norms permit recombination — enforceable-or-not non-competes, trade-secret and inevitable-disclosure doctrine, at-will norms, spinoff equity conventions, and local risk-capital density.
conditions.why_it_matters: This condition carries a second natural experiment — same technology, same bust, same decade, opposite labour institutions, opposite outcome — and it forces a correction to how the operator states the human-capital channel. The bubble does NOT train a generation. US CS bachelor's production ROSE 57% from 37,788 in 1999-2000 to an all-time peak of 59,488 in 2003-04, then fell 36% to 37,992 in 2008-09 — still above the bubble-peak year. Master's never once fell below the 1999-2000 level (14,990 to 17,907, up 19%); doctorates more than doubled, 779 to 1,698. What collapsed was enrolment INTENT, a four-year-lagged leading indicator: Taulbee newly declared majors from 15,958 in fall 2000 to 7,952 in fall 2005, HERI/CIRP freshman intentions down roughly 70%. The frenzy-enrolled cohort graduated INTO the bust, in record numbers. L2's durable contribution to labour is LIQUIDATION — dissolving the firm-specific bonds that hold experienced operators in place and making their time cheap — not schooling. Unit 8200 proves the further point that no distress event is required at all: steady-state demobilisation from a standing institution supplies the same input.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Non-compete enforceability and inevitable-disclosure doctrine in the relevant jurisdiction; prevailing spinoff equity norms; density of local early-stage capital. All fixed, published, and observable years before any bust. Babina (2020), Marx et al. (2009) and Fallick et al. (2006) already partly test the prediction that identical shocks in enforcing versus non-enforcing jurisdictions produce different formation rates.
cases_supporting: Silicon Valley: Fairchild spinoffs with founder equity plus venture capital from 1958 onward produced Apple (1976) and Sun (1982) out of the minicomputer decline, a 6-12 year lag.

Unit 8200: pure demobilisation with no crash and no overbuild — Check Point (1993, Gil Shwed), Wiz (2020, Assaf Rappaport), and a $6-7bn annual export sector. Demonstrates that capability release, not financial distress, is the operative variable.

Nokia to Supercell: Finland, 60,000+ layoffs 2008-2013, Supercell founded 2010, Clash of Clans 2012, $10.2bn to Tencent in 2016. Weak causal attribution — Rovio was founded in 2003 and predates the collapse — and the 2-4 year lag violates the operator's 'decades' claim outright.
cases_failing: Route 128 and DEC: same minicomputer overbuild, same decade, but lifetime-employment norms, no spinoff equity rights, proprietary non-transferable architectures and no venture exit path. No third generation; the PC market was captured by IBM and by Intel in Silicon Valley, and DEC was sold to Compaq in 1998 at distressed prices. Matched against Silicon Valley this isolates the labour variable.
Japan 1990-2005: keiretsu structures and lifetime employment prevented spinoff generation and talent redeployment; foreign M&A was under 2% of M&A value until the 2000s.
Soviet Union: no entry, no equity, no recombination — wage suppression and stranded workers instead of firm liquidation.

TELECOM SPECIFICALLY MUST BE DROPPED: there is no public tracing of WorldCom, Global Crossing or 360networks engineers into any third generation, and carrier employment never recovered. The operator may keep the fibre claim; he may not currently keep a telecom skills claim.

conditions.condition: C8 — PHYSICAL COMPLETION AND COMMISSIONING BEFORE CESSATION. The capacity must have been finished and placed in service before the cessation event. Announced, permitted, contracted or partially built capacity has nothing to dislodge.
conditions.why_it_matters: Historically this is the weakest filter in the set — almost every case passes it, so its discriminating power on the corpus is near zero and it is ranked accordingly. It is listed because prospectively it is currently the MOST binding condition on the AI buildout, where a large share of what is described as capacity is announced megawatts, signed leases and queue positions rather than energised racks. A framework used prospectively must not score announced capacity as installed capacity.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Installed and commissioned units versus announced or permitted units, from interconnection records, commissioning filings and asset registers. Trivially observable and routinely ignored.
cases_supporting: Iridium: the full constellation was in orbit and operating before bankruptcy, which is why a $25m restart was even conceivable.
Globalstar: 52 satellites and the gateways complete before the February 2002 filing; constellation transferred to Thermo Capital for $43m in 2003.
Long-haul fibre: strands in the ground and lit or litable.
Merchant CCGT: plants built, commissioned and dispatching.
cases_failing: Teledesic: over $1.2bn raised from Gates and McCaw, 840 satellites scaled to 300, construction halted 1 October 2002 with nothing flown. No asset to transfer, no third generation, capital simply destroyed. The clean null on this condition.
Better Place: $850m raised, $2.25bn valuation, battery-swap network never reached scale; technology abandoned entirely in May 2013.
Fisker: $1.4bn burned including a $529m DOE loan for 2,450 cars; the productive capacity was never completed.

conditions.condition: C9 — SHARED-ASSET INCOMPATIBILITY. This is the ONLY defensible version of the 'different people' clause. Incumbents fail to capture the third order if and only if the third-order business requires shared use of a firm-level asset with the L1/L2 business on incompatible terms — a price book, a tariff, a channel, a depreciation schedule, an installed-base contract, a labour agreement, or a revenue line that would be cannibalised. The shared asset must be NAMED before the outcome is known. Where no such asset exists, predict incumbent capture.
conditions.why_it_matters: This condition determines WHO captures, not WHETHER a third order exists, which is why it ranks last as an emergence filter and first in importance for the operator's actual question. It is the Bresnahan-Greenstein-Henderson test stated ex ante, and it is the only formulation of 'different people' that is not simply an artefact of where the analyst drew the industry boundary. Its failing-case list is the direct refutation of the operator's clause: in five well-documented cases with no incompatible shared asset, the incumbent captured the third order outright.
conditions.how_to_observe_it: Before the outcome, write down the specific firm-level asset and the specific incompatibility, with the contract, tariff or accounting mechanism that creates it. If you cannot name one in a sentence, score FAIL and predict incumbent capture. Confirm afterwards with the utilisation test, not with the identity of the buyer.
cases_supporting: Incumbent carriers versus Cogent and Level 3: incumbents could not sell transit at the written-down price without cannibalising private-line revenue and breaching their own tariffs. Named, specific, and it held.

Motorola versus Iridium Satellite LLC: a consumer channel and a $45m/month cost structure that could not be shed inside the existing entity. Boeing at $3.5m/month was necessarily a different balance sheet.
DEC versus the PC: a $200,000-minicomputer sales force could not sell a $2,000 box. Named shared asset, incompatible terms, and DEC duly failed.
cases_failing: AWS: no incompatible shared asset — Amazon's retail and AWS shared infrastructure compatibly, and the incumbent captured the third order. Combined with the documented 2003 Black/Pinkham origin containing no bandwidth or capacity reasoning at all, and Vogels calling the excess-capacity story a myth, AWS and Azure must be REMOVED from example (b). Cloudflare (2009) is the only well-chosen name on the operator's list.

Google and Netflix: bubble-era firms run by bubble-era people who simply did not die. Same survivorship error class as the round-1 Cogent and Internap correction, and its recurrence indicates the error is systematic.

BASF, Bayer and Hoechst: dye laboratories redeployed to aspirin (1899) and Haber-Bosch (1909) with a 20-30 year lag and zero change of hands. One of the corpus's strongest supporting cases on lag and redeployment, and a flat refutation of the identity clause.
Insull and Commonwealth Edison: built the capacity, engineered the demand that filled it, and outlived the collapse of the parent holding company while keeping the customers.
Ford: electrified Ford's own plant and built Ford's own line. The identity clause fails at every surviving joint of the operator's flagship case.

discriminating_test.falsification_rule:
The framework makes three separable claims. They have different evidentiary standing and must be falsified separately. Anything scored after the outcome is inadmissible AS EVIDENCE FOR the framework, though always admissible against it.

F1 — THE EMERGENCE CLAIM (the core, and the one still live). Register the frame (metered input P, build-justifying price P*, named downstream industry at a stated NAICS level, and PASS/FAIL on all nine conditions) at T0, the date P first crosses below P* and stays. Then:
(a) FALSIFIED BY INSUFFICIENCY if a case scoring PASS on C1, C2 and C3 shows the capacity scrapped, mothballed, or below 20% utilisation ten years after T0, with no business class existing whose unit economics were negative at P* and are positive at realised P. One such case defeats the joint-sufficiency claim.
(b) FALSIFIED BY LOSS OF NECESSITY if a case scoring FAIL on C1, C2 or C3 nonetheless produces that business class at scale. Each such case defeats the necessity of the specific condition it violates, and must be attributed to a named condition rather than absorbed by the framework as a variant.
(c) FALSIFIED AS A RESET if P recovers to P* within five years of T0 without an intervening new-build cycle. In that case the capacity was simply absorbed and the episode is an ordinary inventory cycle wearing a technological costume.

F2 — THE IDENTITY CLAIM ('different people'). This has ALREADY RETURNED A NEGATIVE and does not need to be re-run. Klepper and Simons are 4/4 the other way with effect sizes of 76-90% in exit hazard; Chandy and Tellis put ~74% of post-1945 radical innovation with incumbents; and in the operator's own exemplar list AWS, Google and Netflix are bubble-era firms run by bubble-era people, Salesforce was founded February 1999 inside the frenzy, Illumina April 1998, DJI and Anker during the shanzhai boom, and Tesla in 2003 before Cleantech 1.0. The honest move is retraction, not further testing. If the operator insists on retaining it, the pre-registration requirement is absolute: fix the industry boundary (SIC/NAICS level, or Gort's product-market definition) before scoring cohort identity, and if the scoring flips under any other reasonable boundary choice, drop the feature. It will flip.

F3 — THE MECHANISM CLAIM, i.e. that this is anything other than ordinary fire-sale value destruction. This is the discriminator the framework currently lacks, and it is the most dangerous test on the list. The framework and Shleifer-Vishny predict the SAME observable — assets exiting the incumbent class in a bust — with OPPOSITE welfare signs. Two tests separate them, and both must be passed:
(i) POST-TRANSFER UTILISATION (Bernstein-Colonnelli-Iverson design): physical utilisation of the transferred capacity must RISE, in contrast to their general finding that liquidation lowers utilisation. Iridium passes (switched off in 2000, profitable by 2005, 19% EBITDA growth in 2010, $135m free cash flow). Ebone passes (dark network relit, $2.3bn exit). Aerospace 1988-95 fails.
(ii) INSIDER-PREMIUM SIGN: estimate Ramey and Shapiro's lambda_insider on the transfers. The framework requires it NEGATIVE (outsiders pay more) in cases it claims and positive in cases it does not. If lambda_insider is uniformly positive across all cases, the framework can never be distinguished from ordinary fire-sale value destruction and should be abandoned as a mechanism claim regardless of how well F1 performs.

THE HIGHEST-PRIORITY LIVE FALSIFIER: CHINA POST-2015. Solar, EV, battery, fibre and property overbuild produced dominant downstream firms with essentially no loss recognition and no title transfer, the January 2024 Hong Kong liquidation order against Evergrande being largely unenforceable onshore. If confirmed, C1 must be restated at the level of REALISED INPUT PRICE rather than legal alienability or loss recognition — i.e. any institution that forces capacity to be sold below its embedded capital cost qualifies, including state-tolerated below-cost competition. Note carefully that this restatement WEAKENS the framework toward tautology (it would make C1 read 'the price fell because the price fell') and should be resisted unless the evidence compels it. This is the single most urgent piece of unfinished work.

A SECOND, SMALLER FALSIFIER AGAINST THE CORPUS ITSELF: the corpus codes US nuclear as a strong null on C1. That coding should be re-examined. Between roughly 1999 and 2002 a genuine merchant consolidation occurred — Entergy, Exelon and Dominion acquiring single-unit plants from vertically integrated utilities at low dollars per kW against multi-billion-dollar build costs — and fleet capacity factors rose from roughly 60% in the 1980s to near 90% by the early 2000s, which is precisely the utilisation signature F3(i) demands. Verify the transaction prices before relying on either coding. If it holds, nuclear moves from FAIL-C1 to a qualified PASS, and the corpus contains a scoring error in the direction that flatters the operator's null cases.

TWO PRE-REGISTERED CORPUS RE-SCORINGS THAT WOULD SETTLE MUCH OF THIS QUICKLY: (1) split Eisfeldt-Rampini's reallocation measure into going-concern transactions between solvent firms versus transfers arising from cessation, Chapter 7 or section 363 sales; the framework requires the entire 0.58 procyclical correlation to sit in the first bucket and the second to be acyclical or countercyclical. If the second is also procyclical at conventional significance, the framework loses its main defence. (2) Run the Caballero-Hoshi-Kashyap congestion specification on US airlines 1990-2010; C3 requires a significantly negative coefficient, unlike the near-zero the authors report for US Compustat 1995-2004.
discriminating_test.reference_frame_fix:
THE DIAGNOSIS. The ordinal is indexical because the framework tried to count generations of TECHNOLOGY from an origin, and technology has no canonical origin — every L3 is some other case's L1. Worse, the stress test on canonical example (a) shows the true topology is not even a chain: David and Wright describe "the technological confluence, or convergence, of electrification with other trajectories of industrial innovation," and note explicitly that automated materials handling did not require electrification. In a lattice of converging trajectories, "which layer is this" has no answer in principle, not merely in practice. No amount of care in counting fixes a counting problem whose object is not linear.

THE FIX: STOP COUNTING TECHNOLOGIES. COUNT CLAIMS ON ONE METERED CAPACITY. Call it the Input-Price Frame. Before any layer assignment, register four things in writing with a timestamp:

1. THE METERED INPUT. A specific, quotable unit price P(t) for a physical or legal capacity: dollars per Mbps-month of IP transit; dollars per satellite voice-minute; dollars per kW-year of dispatchable capacity; dollars per litre of ethanol distillation capacity; dollars per GPU-hour of a named accelerator class; dollars per MW-year of energised, interconnected datacentre capacity. It must be a published or contractible series, not a narrative.

2. THE BUILD-JUSTIFYING PRICE P*. The price the L2 capital's own pro formas required in order to return cost of capital. This is a HISTORICAL FACT, not an analyst choice — it is recoverable from prospectuses, project-finance models, auction bids, rate cases, take-or-pay terms, and the useful-life and depreciation assumptions in filed accounts. Fixing P* from documents rather than from judgement is what makes the frame non-indexical.

3. THE THRESHOLD BUSINESS CLASS. A named class of downstream business, at a stated NAICS or SIC level with a customer set distinct from the builders', whose gross margin is negative at P* and positive at some P below P*. Named before the outcome.

4. THE CONDITION SCORECARD. PASS/FAIL on C1-C9, recorded before the outcome window opens.

Then the ordinal is defined by ENUMERATING THE BALANCE SHEETS THAT HAVE OWNED THE ECONOMICS OF THAT ONE CAPACITY:
- FIRST ORDER: the builder, who underwrote at P*.
- SECOND ORDER: the claimant who takes the write-down — bondholders, receiver, acquiring creditor, or the state where losses are forced administratively.
- THIRD ORDER: the operator or consumer whose business exists only because P is now below P*.

"Third order" therefore means the THIRD CLAIM ON A SINGLE NAMED CAPACITY, not the third generation of a technology. Claims on an asset are enumerable and finite. Technologies are not.

WHY THIS ACTUALLY TERMINATES THE RECURSION. You may run the frame again on a DIFFERENT metered input, but you cannot run it again on the SAME one, because once the capacity is held at written-down basis by an operator whose business works, there is no further write-down to harvest. The number of write-downs on a given asset is finite and typically one. That is the endogenous stopping rule round 1 said the framework lacked, and it comes from the accounting, not from a judgement about generativity decay.

FOUR CONSEQUENCES, AT LEAST TWO OF THEM UNWELCOME.

(a) THE ASSEMBLY LINE DROPS OUT. There is no single metered input price whose collapse the assembly line consumed. Under the repaired frame it is not third order of anything — which is exactly how David and Wright, the framework's own authorities, classify it. Highland Park in 1913 ran on electric GROUP drive off Ford's own gas-steam powerhouse, the shallow no-payoff configuration; unit drive and single-storey linear layout reached Ford in the 1920s, with the multi-storey to single-storey branch-plant switch dating to 1922, and Biggs records that few machines ran on individual motors in Ford's factories even as late as 1918. The line sat BETWEEN two phases of the reorganisation and helped pull the second. That a repair excludes the operator's flagship example is evidence the repair is doing work rather than accommodating.

(b) THE MECHANISM IS INPUT-PRICE RESET, NOT ASSET TRANSFER. This follows directly from anchoring on a price series rather than a title chain, and it is what the evidence supports: Netflix and Cloudflare bought SERVICES priced off written-down assets; Cogent, Level 3 and Zayo bought the assets and earn utility returns. Yahoo!BB got the reset with zero change in ownership, via mandated local-loop unbundling at Y990 per month for 8Mbps from September 2001. Title is one instrument among four; price is the invariant.

(c) THE FRAME EXCLUDES CANONICAL EXAMPLE (b)'S CLOUD HALF ON ITS OWN TERMS. Register P as dollars per GB of transport and the ASP-to-SaaS natural experiment settles it: bandwidth was under 1% of ASP revenue even at peak-1998 transit prices, so a 100x fall in a line item that small cannot bind; Salesforce was founded March 1999 on input prices identical to Corio and USinternetworking and survived on multi-tenancy; AWS's documented 2003 Black/Pinkham origin contains no bandwidth reasoning whatsoever. The frame correctly admits the video/CDN chain and correctly rejects the cloud chain. It also exposes the framework's missing slot: streaming required DOCSIS 3.0 and FiOS at roughly $23bn from incumbent cash flow, plus H.264, Flash's December 2007 H.264 build, Silverlight, Roku and the Xbox — a mandatory, capital-intensive, NON-bubble intermediate layer that the frame has no place for and must acknowledge.

(d) WHAT THE FRAME IS NOT. It is not a description of how technology develops. It describes the fate of one metered capacity and the margins of one downstream class. Anyone reading it as a succession theory will be wrong, and the lattice problem is untouched by it — the frame sidesteps the lattice rather than solving it.

WORKED REGISTRATION FOR THE AI BUILDOUT, to be lodged before the outcome. Metered inputs: dollars per GPU-hour of a named accelerator class; dollars per MW-year of energised interconnected capacity; dollars per million tokens at a named quality tier. P* is recoverable TODAY from hyperscaler depreciation schedules and useful-life assumptions, neocloud lease and take-or-pay terms, and the pro formas behind PPAs and interconnection agreements. Present scorecard: C8 is currently the binding failure — most announced capacity is not energised, and announced megawatts must not be scored as installed capacity. C1 is mixed and checkable now by reading documents: interconnection queue positions and many PPAs are non-transferable on default, which is the German UMTS pattern; datacentre shells and substations under project finance generally are transferable, which is the NextWave pattern. C4 and C5 give the sharpest prediction available: grid interconnects, substations, transmission and shells are substrate with flat-to-rising real replacement cost and will transfer and appreciate in use, while accelerator fleets are overlay with steeply deflating replacement cost and will fail the reset-persistence test — a distressed 2028 buyer of 2025 silicon gets no durable advantage, exactly as a distressed 2012 buyer of 2010 solar got none.
